intro.en: Core surgical and minor procedures in obstetrics and gynaecology, detailing operative steps, clinical indications, anatomical landmarks, complications, and viva examination spotters.

title.en: Abdominal Incisions in Gynaecology and Obstetrics

items.summary: Surgical entry routes through the anterior abdominal wall classified into vertical, transverse, and oblique orientations based on clinical indications and anatomical planes.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Surgical incisions created through the anterior abdominal wall for pelvic and abdominal exploration.
Primary types comprise vertical cuts, transverse incisions, and oblique entries selected by operative urgency, pathology size, and exposure requirements.

groups.label: Vertical incisions
bullets: Midline vertical incision provides universal access for almost all exploratory laparotomies and emergency pelvic surgeries.
Paramedian incision sited 2 to 5 cm lateral to midline provides lateral exposure for renal, adrenal, splenic, or adnexal masses.

groups.label: Transverse incisions
bullets: Pfannenstiel incision located 2 cm superior to the symphysis pubis is standard for lower segment caesarean section (LSCS) and benign hysterectomy.
Maylard muscle-splitting incision placed 3 to 8 cm above Pfannenstiel from anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to ASIS is favoured by gynaecological oncologists.
Cherney incision detaches the rectus abdominis tendons from the pubic crest to visualise the retropubic space of Retzius and pelvic sidewalls.
Joel-Cohen straight transverse incision sited 3 cm above the symphysis pubis offers rapid entry for caesarean delivery.
Misgav-Ladakh technique placed 3 cm below the interspinous line prioritises minimal sharp dissection for swift, low-morbidity caesarean birth.
Kustner curvilinear incision 5 cm above the pubic crest exposes the pelvic cavity but carries high risk of haematoma and limited view.

groups.label: Oblique incisions
bullets: McBurney incision positioned at the junction of the lateral third and medial two thirds of the spinoumbilical line enables appendicectomy.
Kocher subcostal incision beginning 2 to 5 cm inferior to the xiphoid process accesses the biliary tree, liver, and spleen.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Patient positioned supine; bladder evacuated using an indwelling Foley catheter to avoid iatrogenic cystotomy.
Skin prepared with antiseptic chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine solution and draped under strict surgical asepsis.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Midline incision traverses skin, Camper and Scarpa subcutaneous fascia, linea alba, transversalis fascia, and parietal peritoneum.
Paramedian entry divides the anterior rectus sheath, retracts rectus muscle laterally, and incises posterior sheath or transversalis fascia and peritoneum.
Pfannenstiel cuts skin and rectus sheath transversely, mobilises rectus bellies vertically, and enters peritoneum in the vertical plane.
Maylard cuts through rectus abdominis transversely and splits transversus abdominis fibres bluntly before opening the peritoneal cavity.
Cherney incises anterior sheath transversely, sharply divides rectus tendons off the pubic bone, and re-anchors them securely during closure.
Joel-Cohen incises skin and anterior sheath transversely followed by blunt finger traction laterally and digital peritoneal entry.
Misgav-Ladakh enters rectus sheath sharply for 3 to 4 cm, expands it with fingers craniocaudally, exteriorises the uterus, and repairs myometrium in 1 layer.
McBurney divides external oblique aponeurosis along Langer lines, splits internal oblique and transversus abdominis bluntly, and opens peritoneum.
Kocher divides anterior rectus sheath, rectus muscle, internal oblique, transversus abdominis, transversalis fascia, and peritoneum.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Wound haematoma, seroma formation, surgical site infection, and incisional hernia.
Paramedian entry risks medial rectus atrophy from denervation, prolonged operative duration, and asymmetric abdominal wall scarring.
Maylard incision risks significant intraoperative haemorrhage and injury to inferior epigastric blood vessels.
Oblique incisions risk injury to iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves leading to sensory deficits and secondary inguinal herniation.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Provide multimodal analgesia and monitor wound dressings for bleeding or strike-through discharge.
Encourage early ambulation and thromboprophylaxis to prevent venous thromboembolism (VTE).
Inspect healing surgical scar and advise against heavy lifting or strenuous exertion for 6 weeks.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Midline vertical incision provides the swiftest abdominal access and easiest cranial extension during critical surgical emergencies.
Transverse incisions run parallel to Langer cleavage lines, conferring superior cosmetic appearance, reduced pain, and lower herniation rates.
Closure of Cherney incision requires secure non-absorbable or delayed-absorbable reattachment of rectus tendons to the anterior rectus sheath.

viva.q: What anatomical layers are incised during a midline vertical laparotomy below the umbilicus?
viva.a: Skin, subcutaneous fatty tissue (Camper and Scarpa fascia), linea alba, transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat, and parietal peritoneum. Note that no posterior rectus sheath exists below the arcuate line.

viva.q: What is the key anatomical landmark and dissection plane distinguishing the Cherney incision?
viva.a: The Cherney incision involves transverse incision of the anterior rectus sheath followed by sharp detachment of the rectus abdominis muscle tendons from their insertion on the pubic symphysis, exposing the retropubic space.

viva.q: Which major blood vessels are at risk during a Maylard transverse muscle-cutting incision?
viva.a: The inferior epigastric arteries and veins running along the lateral aspect of the rectus abdominis muscles must be identified and securely ligated to prevent catastrophic retroperitoneal haemorrhage.

title.en: Suture Materials in Obstetrics and Gynaecology

items.summary: Surgical filaments categorized by biologic fate, structural configuration, and raw origin, selected according to tissue tensile requirements and healing dynamics.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Sterile filaments utilised for tissue approximation, vascular ligation, and wound repair across pelvic and obstetric procedures.
Classified primarily by degradation profile into absorbable versus non-absorbable, structural design into monofilament versus braided multifilament, and origin into natural versus synthetic.

groups.label: Absorbable sutures
bullets: Plain catgut: Straw coloured natural collagen degraded enzymatically in 18 to 21 days; maintains tensile hold for 7 days; utilised for superficial vascular ligation and mucosal approximation.

Chromic catgut: Brown coloured bovine or ovine gut treated with chromium salts; retains strength for 10 to 14 days and absorbs fully by 90 days; applied in pelvic surgery, bladder repair, and soft tissue closure.
Polyglactin 910 (Vicryl): Violet braided synthetic copolymer; retains 84% strength at 2 weeks and 20% at 4 weeks, absorbing by 90 days via hydrolysis; standard for caesarean uterine closure.

Polydioxanone (PDS): Violet monofilament synthetic polymer; retains 80% strength at 2 weeks and 40% at 8 weeks, absorbing by 210 days; preferred for high-tension repairs including third and fourth-degree perineal tears.
Polyglycolic acid (PGA / Dexon): Braided synthetic filament degraded by hydrolysis in 90 to 120 days with minimal tissue reaction.
Rapid polyglactin 910 (Vicryl Rapide): Irradiated fast-absorbing synthetic thread absorbed within 2 weeks; favoured for episiotomy and perineal skin closure.
Polyglecaprone 25 (Monocryl): Synthetic monofilament absorbed within 90 to 120 days; ideal for subcuticular aesthetic skin closure.
Polytrimethylene carbonate (Maxon): Monofilament synthetic suture absorbing completely within 180 to 210 days for long-term fascial support.

groups.label: Non-absorbable sutures
bullets: Polypropylene (Prolene): Blue synthetic monofilament polyolefin with minimal tissue reactivity; ideal for rectus sheath abdominal fascial closure and hernia repair, even in infected fields.
Nylon (Polyamide): Blue or black synthetic monofilament with low tissue reaction; utilised for skin suturing and delicate plastic or microsurgical repairs.
Silk: Black or white natural braided protein fibroin derived from silkworm cocoons; provides excellent knot handling but induces marked acute inflammation.
Specialised polymers: Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) prevents postoperative tissue adhesions; polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) provides improved knot security and handling over polypropylene.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Select needle curvature, needle point (round-bodied for visceral soft tissues, cutting/reverse-cutting for tough skin/sheath), and thread gauge according to target tissue density.
Maintain strict aseptic handling, avoiding instrumental crushing of monofilament strands to prevent structural weakening.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Inspect packaging to verify suture gauge, expiry date, needle curvature, and filament properties prior to opening.
Mount needle on the needle holder at the junction of its anterior two thirds and posterior one third.
Drive needle perpendicularly through tissue margins following the natural arc of the needle without excessive lateral torque.
Secure knot using square throws, ensuring appropriate throw count based on filament memory and friction characteristics.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Suture knot slippage or breakage resulting in wound dehiscence or secondary intra-abdominal haemorrhage.
Excessive inflammatory tissue reaction, sterile suture abscess, stitch sinuses, or delayed granuloma formation (marked with natural silk and plain catgut).
Bacterial colonization and capillary fluid wicking through multifilament braided sutures in contaminated wound beds.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Monitor surgical incisions for signs of erythema, induration, or purulent exudate indicating suture tract infection.
Plan timely removal of non-absorbable skin sutures between postoperative days 5 and 7 to prevent permanent cross-hatching marks.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Monofilament sutures slide smoothly with minimal tissue drag and harbour no pathogens, but exhibit high memory and necessitate additional knot throws.
Multifilament braided sutures provide superior pliability and exceptional knot security, but exhibit capillary wicking that may propagate surgical site sepsis.
Vicryl 1 is the standard choice for uterine hysterotomy closure, while Prolene 1 is the preferred non-absorbable choice for rectus sheath reconstruction.

viva.q: What are the key structural and clinical distinctions between monofilament and multifilament sutures?
viva.a: Monofilaments have a single smooth strand with minimal tissue drag but high memory. Multifilaments are braided, offering superior knot security and handling but carry capillary fluid wicking risk.

viva.q: Which suture material is preferred for closing third- and fourth-degree perineal tears, and why?
viva.a: Polydioxanone (PDS) is preferred because it is an absorbable monofilament that maintains prolonged tensile strength (up to 8 weeks) to support slow-healing anal sphincter muscle without promoting bacterial wicking.

viva.q: How do plain catgut and polyglactin 910 differ in mechanism of tissue absorption?
viva.a: Plain catgut undergoes enzymatic breakdown by tissue proteases with marked inflammatory reaction, whereas polyglactin 910 (Vicryl) degrades predictably via chemical hydrolysis with minimal surrounding tissue reaction.

title.en: Post-Operative Care for Major and Minor Surgery

items.summary: Systematic clinical management following major or minor pelvic interventions designed to optimise analgesia, prevent thromboembolism, support wound healing, and restore physiological function.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Structured perioperative monitoring and supportive therapy implemented immediately following completion of surgical procedures.
Distinguished into comprehensive intensive pathways for major pelvic laparotomies and streamlined recovery protocols for minor day-care operations.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Routine post-procedural management following major abdominal and vaginal operations including caesarean delivery, hysterectomy, and myomectomy.
Outpatient recovery protocols following minor gynaecological interventions including cervical biopsy, suction evacuation, and diagnostic hysteroscopy.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Transfer patient safely from operative table to recovery bed maintaining warm blankets and hemodynamic monitoring.
Position patient supine with head elevation or lateral recovery posture according to anaesthetic recovery and airway stability.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Administer effective analgesia utilising epidural infusions or patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) with opioid or non-opioid regimens for major operations.
Institute deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis through calibrated graduated compression stockings, early assisted ambulation, and low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH).
Deliver prophylactic or therapeutic intravenous antibiotics according to institutional surgical antimicrobial protocols.
Maintain indwelling urethral catheterisation to accurately document hourly urine output and protect surgical repairs from bladder distension.
Administer intravenous crystalloid hydration until bowel motility returns and the patient tolerates unrestricted oral fluids.
Inspect wound dressings systematically for haematoma or purulent discharge, ensuring clean and dry conditions.
For minor procedures, prescribe simple oral analgesics, provide short-course antibiotics where indicated, and encourage rapid resumption of baseline daily activity.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) presenting as deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or life-threatening pulmonary embolism (PE).
Urinary tract infection, acute urinary retention, or bladder atony following catheter removal.
Surgical site infection, wound dehiscence, or intra-abdominal collection formation.
Paralytic ileus or secondary bowel injury secondary to surgical manipulation and opioid analgesia.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Counsel patients undergoing major pelvic surgery to avoid strenuous physical lifting and vigorous exertion for 6 weeks.
Instruct patients to abstain from vaginal intercourse for 6 weeks to allow complete vault, cervical, and pelvic floor healing.
Schedule outpatient wound review at 1 to 2 weeks and comprehensive gynaecological examination at 6 weeks.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Active multimodal thromboprophylaxis combining mechanical compression with pharmacological LMWH significantly reduces perioperative maternal mortality.
Early mobilisation within 24 hours of major laparotomy accelerates gastrointestinal recovery, decreases pulmonary atelectasis, and mitigates thromboembolic risk.

viva.q: What are the core components of venous thromboprophylaxis following major gynaecological surgery?
viva.a: A multimodal strategy combining graduated mechanical compression stockings, pneumatic calf compression devices, early aggressive ambulation, and weight-adjusted low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH).

viva.q: What specific postoperative lifestyle advice must be provided to a patient following major pelvic surgery?
viva.a: Advise the patient to avoid heavy lifting or strenuous exertion for 6 weeks, abstain from vaginal sexual intercourse for 6 weeks, maintain wound hygiene, and seek immediate care if high fever or abnormal bleeding occurs.

items.summary: Operative abdominal delivery of the fetus, placenta, and membranes through a transverse hysterotomy incision sited in the lower uterine segment.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Surgical birth procedure where neonate and placenta are extracted via laparotomy and uterine incision made into the lower uterine segment (LUS).
Primary operative method chosen over classical vertical hysterotomy owing to minimal bleeding, easy reperitonealisation, and lower rupture risk in future gestations.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Fetal compromise: Non-reassuring fetal status, acute fetal distress, umbilical cord prolapse, and abnormal presentations such as persistent transverse lie or breech.
Maternal-fetal cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD) and failed induction of labour.
Previous uterine scar risks: Three or more previous caesarean deliveries, prior classical caesarean scar, or documented uterine rupture.
Placental complications: Major placenta praevia, placenta accreta spectrum, or placental abruption.
Maternal medical conditions: Uncontrolled HIV infection with high viral load, active primary genital herpes simplex virus in the third trimester, and severe cardiac disease.
Mechanical obstruction: Obstructing cervical leiomyoma, cervical carcinoma, and fetal macrosomia with estimated fetal weight exceeding 5 kg.
Multiple pregnancy: Monoamniotic twin gestation.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Patient positioned supine with a 15-degree left lateral pelvic tilt using a wedge to relieve aortocaval compression.
Indwelling Foley catheter placed to empty the urinary bladder and decompress it below the surgical field.
Administered under spinal or general anaesthesia adhering to strict surgical asepsis and skin disinfection.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Perform transverse suprapubic skin incision (Pfannenstiel or Joel-Cohen) and enter abdominal cavity in layers.
Identify and incise the uterovesical peritoneal fold, gently deflecting the urinary bladder inferiorly with a Doyen retractor.
Make a curvilinear transverse hysterotomy incision in the lower uterine segment and expand it bluntly with fingers or scissors.
Rupture exposed amniotic membranes and introduce dominant hand into the lower segment beneath the fetal occiput.
Deliver the fetal head gently using the hand as a vectis while an assistant applies steady transabdominal fundal pressure.
Deliver fetal shoulders and trunk; double-clamp the umbilical cord with two pairs of long forceps and divide it cleanly between clamps.
Hand neonate to neonatologist and administer 10 units of intravenous oxytocin (Syntocinon) to stimulate vigorous myometrial contraction.
Deliver placenta and attached amniotic membranes en toto using controlled cord traction.
Secure uterine wound angles with Allis tissue forceps and grasp bleeding hysterotomy edges with Green-Armytage clamps.
Close the hysterotomy incision in two continuous layers using absorbable synthetic suture (Vicryl No. 1).
Verify meticulous haemostasis in both paracolic gutters, clear pelvic clots, confirm surgical swab and instrument counts, and close the abdominal wall anatomically.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Intraoperative haemorrhage, atonic postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), need for emergency blood transfusion, and peripartum hysterectomy.
Iatrogenic laceration to the urinary bladder, ureters, or bowel loops.
Postoperative deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism, urinary retention, and surgical site or urinary tract infections.
Late sequelae: Uterine scar dehiscence or rupture in subsequent gestations, secondary infertility, and morbidly adherent placenta accreta spectrum.
Neonatal risks: Transient tachypnoea of the newborn (TTN) and accidental fetal scalpel lacerations.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Monitor vital signs, vaginal lochial flow, and uterine fundal firmness every 15 minutes during the immediate recovery phase.
Provide scheduled multimodal analgesia and maintain intravenous maintenance hydration until oral fluid tolerance.
Remove urinary catheter within 12 to 24 hours, encourage early ambulation, and initiate thromboprophylaxis.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: For a high floating fetal head, application of obstetric forceps (such as Wrigley blades) through the hysterotomy assists controlled cranial delivery.
In deeply impacted fetal heads in occipito-anterior or transverse position, Patwardhan technique delivers shoulders and trunk first before head extraction.
In occipito-posterior impacted heads, Modified Patwardhan technique hooks the anterior arm to deliver anterior shoulder, then lower limbs, trunk, and head.

viva.q: What is the Patwardhan technique during difficult caesarean delivery, and when is it employed?
viva.a: It is an operative manoeuvre for delivering a deeply impacted fetal head in occipito-anterior or transverse lie by delivering the fetal shoulders and trunk first through the hysterotomy, followed by delivering the head from below.

viva.q: Why is oxytocin 10 units administered intravenously immediately following delivery of the infant during LSCS?
viva.a: Intravenous oxytocin produces rhythmic, sustained myometrial contractions that hasten physiological placental separation, minimize third-stage blood loss, and prevent primary atonic postpartum haemorrhage.

viva.q: Name three absolute maternal or fetal indications for performing lower segment caesarean section.
viva.a: Major placenta praevia covering the internal cervical os, complete cephalopelvic disproportion, and umbilical cord prolapse with a live viable fetus.

image.brief: Intraoperative surgical illustration of a lower segment caesarean section showing transverse lower uterine incision, operator hand elevating fetal head as a vectis, and bladder reflected inferiorly by a Doyen retractor.

items.summary: Minor surgical intervention using negative vacuum pressure to evacuate retained or abnormal intrauterine gestational contents through a dilated cervix.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Therapeutic transcervical procedure utilising negative mechanical pressure to aspirate conceptive tissues from the uterine cavity.
Gold standard surgical modality for first-trimester pregnancy evacuation, carrying significantly lower perforation risks than sharp metallic curettage.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Missed miscarriage where retained non-viable intrauterine pregnancy requires prompt surgical clearance.
Incomplete miscarriage presenting with active vaginal bleeding and retained conceptive tissue.
Gestational trophoblastic disease including complete or partial hydatidiform molar pregnancy.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Patient placed in lithotomy position under regional, paracervical, or general anaesthesia with full surgical asepsis.
Perform bimanual examination to confirm uterine size, flexion, version, and gestational duration prior to instrumentation.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Insert a Sims speculum to depress the posterior vaginal wall and expose the cervix clearly.
Grasp the anterior cervical lip gently with a sponge-holding forceps (avoid vulsellum or sharp tenaculum to prevent lacerating soft pregnant cervical tissue).
Pass a calibrated blunt uterine sound gently to the fundus to confirm uterine axial cavity length.
Dilate the endocervical canal sequentially using Hegar dilators up to approximately 10 mm in diameter.
Introduce an appropriate suction cannula (8 to 10 mm diameter) through the internal os advancing gently to the fundus.
Connect cannula to suction source and apply negative aspiration pressure calibrated at 60 mm Hg.
Rotate and advance the suction curette systematically 2 to 3 times across all uterine surfaces until cavity feels empty and gritty.
Administer parenteral oxytocic agents as required to stimulate myometrial contractions and control post-evacuation bleeding.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Intraoperative haemorrhage, acute cervical laceration, uterine wall perforation, and accidental visceral trauma to bladder or bowel loops.
Postoperative pelvic sepsis, acute endometritis, and secondary urinary tract infection.
Late reproductive complications including intrauterine synechiae (Asherman syndrome) and cervical incompetence.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Observe patient in day-care recovery monitoring vital signs and assessing vaginal bleeding every 30 minutes for 2 to 4 hours.
Prescribe oral prophylactic antibiotics, simple analgesics, and administer Rh anti-D immunoglobulin to Rh-negative unsensitised women.
Instruct patient to report immediately if heavy vaginal bleeding, severe cramping, or foul vaginal discharge develops.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Never grasp the soft pregnant cervix with a toothed vulsellum or tenaculum, which readily tears vascular cervical tissue; always use a sponge-holding ring forceps.
The tactile sign of completion is a gritty uterine sensation accompanied by myometrial gripping of the suction cannula and bubble-free red foam in the aspiration tubing.

viva.q: Why is a sponge-holding forceps preferred over a vulsellum when stabilising the cervix during suction and evacuation?
viva.a: The pregnant cervix is softened and highly vascular under gestational hormones; a sharp toothed vulsellum or tenaculum easily tears and lacerates cervical lips, whereas a smooth sponge-holding forceps holds atraumatically.

viva.q: What clinical and tactile signs indicate complete emptying of the uterine cavity during suction curettage?
viva.a: A distinct gritty sensation felt through the curette, the uterine cavity contracting tightly around the cannula, and the appearance of pink foam with absence of further gestational tissue in the aspiration tubing.

items.summary: Transvaginal placement of a non-absorbable purse-string suture around the cervix at the cervicovaginal junction to reinforce an incompetent internal os.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Simple transvaginal purse-string encirclage of the cervix without anatomical dissection of the bladder reflection.
Standard surgical intervention for managing cervical incompetence and preventing recurrent mid-trimester pregnancy loss.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Documented cervical insufficiency presenting with recurrent painless second-trimester miscarriages or spontaneous preterm births.
Transvaginal ultrasound demonstration of cervical shortening (length less than 25 mm) or internal os funnelling prior to 24 weeks gestation in high-risk women.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Patient placed in lithotomy position under regional or light general anaesthesia.
Perineum and vagina prepared under strict surgical asepsis, ensuring complete urinary bladder emptying.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Expose the cervix with vaginal retractors and grasp the anterior and posterior cervical lips with sponge-holding forceps.
Identify the cervicovaginal junction where vaginal mucosal rugosity transitions into smooth cervical squamous epithelium, marking the level of the internal os.
Insert a non-absorbable suture (such as monofilament polypropylene / Prolene or braided Mersilene) on a large curved needle just deep to the mucosal junction.
Place four deep circumferential submucosal bites around the cervix starting at 12 o'clock and passing sequentially through 3 o'clock, 6 o'clock, 9 o'clock, and exiting at 12 o'clock.
Tie the suture firmly anteriorly to constrict and occlude the internal cervical os to approximately 5 to 10 mm while avoiding mucosal ischemia.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Iatrogenic rupture of fetal membranes and chorioamnionitis.
Cervical laceration, local bleeding, and suture displacement or slippage.
Premature onset of uterine contractions and preterm labour.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Monitor for uterine contractions, vaginal bleeding, or fluid leakage in recovery for 24 hours.
Administer prophylactic tocolysis or progesterone therapy if indicated and advise avoidance of strenuous physical activity.
Schedule elective stitch removal transvaginally at 36 to 37 completed weeks of gestation, or immediately if active labour supervenes.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: McDonald technique does not dissect the bladder reflection off the cervix, making it technically simpler and quicker than the Shirodkar operation.
If active labour contractions establish with the stitch in situ, remove the suture immediately to avoid catastrophic cervical avulsion or annular detachment.

viva.q: What anatomical landmark marks the site of stitch insertion in the McDonald cerclage?
viva.a: The junction between the corrugated vaginal wall rugosity and the smooth cervical mucosa, which closely corresponds to the anatomical level of the internal cervical os.

viva.q: When should an elective McDonald cerclage stitch be removed?
viva.a: Electively at 36 to 37 completed weeks of gestation in the outpatient department without anaesthesia, or immediately upon the onset of regular active labour contractions to prevent severe cervical rupture.

image.brief: Diagram of McDonald cervical cerclage illustrating purse-string non-absorbable suture placed in four circumferential bites at the cervicovaginal junction around the external cervical os.

items.summary: Submucosal transvaginal high cerclage involving anterior and posterior vaginal mucosal dissection and bladder reflection to place a synthetic tape at the internal os.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: High transvaginal cervical cerclage that mobilises the uterovesical fold and reflects the bladder to anchor a submucosal tape at the true level of the internal os.
Anatomical cerclage operation designed by VN Shirodkar providing robust closure of an incompetent cervix.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: History of 3 or more previous spontaneous preterm deliveries.
History of 3 or more consecutive second-trimester miscarriages.
History of 1 or more spontaneous preterm births or second-trimester losses prior to 24 weeks with transvaginal ultrasound showing cervical length under 25 mm before 24 weeks.
Previous failure of low vaginal McDonald cerclage with extensive anatomical cervical laceration or scarring.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Conducted under regional anaesthesia (spinal or epidural) in the lithotomy position under rigorous operating room asepsis.
Ensure empty bladder and verify fetal cardiac viability by ultrasound prior to inducing anaesthesia.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Grasp anterior and posterior lips of the cervix with sponge-holding forceps to exert gentle downward traction.
Identify the cervicovaginal junction demarcating the internal os reflection.
Make a small transverse mucosal incision on the anterior vaginal wall at this junction.
Identify the cervicovesical fascia, dissect the uterovesical fold of peritoneum, and mobilise the bladder superiorly off the anterior cervix.
Create a small counter-incision through the posterior vaginal mucosa at the corresponding level.
Pass a Mersilene tape (or heavy nylon/prolene) submucosally using curved Shirodkar needles from anterior incision laterally around each side to the posterior incision.
Alternatively, pass tape from posterior to anterior to knot posteriorly; cinch the tape snugly to occlude the internal os.
Close the anterior and posterior vaginal mucosal incisions cleanly over the buried knot using absorbable sutures.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Early: Significant intraoperative haemorrhage, cervical lacerations, accidental bladder perforation, iatrogenic membrane rupture, preterm labour, sepsis, and UTI.
Late: Cervical stenosis, cervical dystocia, precipitate labour, recurrent preterm birth, and vesicovaginal or cervicovaginal fistula formation.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Maintain bed rest with fetal heart rate and uterine tone monitoring in the immediate postoperative phase.
Prescribe prophylactic tocolytics and antibiotics according to clinical protocol.
Shirodkar tape may be left in situ for elective caesarean delivery, or removed under regional anaesthesia at 37 weeks if vaginal birth is planned.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Absolute contraindications: Active labour, ruptured membranes, chorioamnionitis, lethal fetal anomalies, acute fetal distress, active vaginal bleeding, and intrauterine fetal demise.
Unlike McDonald cerclage, Shirodkar requires regional anaesthesia for both initial insertion and surgical removal due to its buried submucosal position.
Alternative cerclage procedures include transabdominal cerclage, Wurm (Hefner cross-mattress) technique, and Lash repair.

viva.q: What anatomical dissection step differentiates the Shirodkar cerclage from the McDonald technique?
viva.a: In Shirodkar cerclage, anterior vaginal mucosal incisions are made, the cervicovesical space is opened, and the urinary bladder is mobilised superiorly, enabling the tape to be placed submucosally at the true internal os level.

viva.q: List four absolute contraindications to placing a cervical cerclage.
viva.a: Active labour contractions, premature rupture of membranes, chorioamnionitis or intra-amniotic infection, and unexplained active vaginal haemorrhage.

viva.q: Why does Shirodkar cerclage removal typically necessitate anaesthesia?
viva.a: Because the synthetic tape and its securing knot are completely buried beneath the re-approximated anterior and posterior vaginal mucosa, requiring surgical incisional exposure under regional anaesthesia.

image.brief: Medical anatomical illustration of Shirodkar cervical cerclage showing reflected urinary bladder anteriorly, transverse mucosal nicks, and curved needle guiding Mersilene tape submucosally around the cervix at the internal os.

items.summary: Emergency intra-uterine manual manoeuvre performed under anaesthesia to separate and extract an unseparated or retained placenta following childbirth.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Intrauterine manual intervention to separate the retroplacental cleavage plane and extract the retained placenta when spontaneous third-stage delivery fails.
Emergency obstetric procedure required to prevent catastrophic postpartum haemorrhage and intrauterine sepsis.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Failure of placental expulsion after 30 minutes following delivery of the infant during the third stage of labour.
Poor uterine contractility and tone after delivery with active third-stage haemorrhage.
Simple adherent placenta failing to detach despite active physiological and pharmacologic management.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Patient placed in lithotomy position under general anaesthesia or effective regional block with strict surgical asepsis.
Ensure wide-bore intravenous access, availability of cross-matched blood products, and prophylactic uterotonic infusions.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Separate the labia gently with the fingers of the non-dominant hand.
Form the dominant hand into a cone shape, lubricate with sterile antiseptic, and advance it slowly through the vagina and dilated cervix into the uterine cavity.
Place non-dominant hand firmly over the abdominal wall to grasp and stabilise the uterine fundus, counter-guiding the intrauterine hand.
Follow the umbilical cord upwards to reach the attached placental margin.
Insert the ulnar border and dorsum of the fingers into the cleavage plane between the placenta and myometrial wall.
Perform continuous, gentle side-to-side slicing and sawing motions of the extended fingers to shear the placenta cleanly off the uterine wall.
Once complete detachment is achieved, grasp the placenta and extract it through the cervix under controlled cord traction while administering oxytocics.
Re-explore the uterine cavity digitally to verify complete evacuation and confirm firm fundal contraction.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Intraoperative haemorrhage, acute uterine inversion, uterine perforation, and need for emergency peripartum hysterectomy.
Postoperative endometritis, retained placental cotyledons, and pelvic sepsis.
Late risk of placenta praevia and morbidly adherent placenta accreta spectrum in future pregnancies.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Administer a continuous infusion of intravenous oxytocin to maintain robust myometrial tone and prevent secondary haemorrhage.
Prescribe therapeutic broad-spectrum antibiotics to reduce intrauterine infectious morbidity.
Monitor vital signs, pad saturation, and uterine firmness closely in high-dependency recovery.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: External abdominal fundal counter-pressure is essential to stabilize the uterus and prevent accidental uterine rupture or acute inversion during manipulation.
Never attempt forceful tearing or avulsion if a plane cannot be established; dense unseparated myometrial invasion indicates placenta accreta spectrum requiring laparotomy.

viva.q: What is the primary role of the external non-dominant hand during manual removal of the placenta?
viva.a: The external hand grasps the fundus transabdominally to stabilise the uterus, provide counter-traction against intrauterine forces, guide the internal fingers, and prevent acute uterine inversion or fundal perforation.

viva.q: When is the diagnosis of retained placenta made following vaginal delivery?
viva.a: When the placenta fails to deliver within 30 minutes following birth of the infant with active third-stage management, or within 60 minutes with physiological management.

image.brief: Obstetric diagram of manual removal of the placenta showing cone-shaped internal hand cleaving the retroplacental plane with a slicing motion while the external hand stabilizes the uterine fundus transabdominally.

items.summary: Uterine-sparing brace compression suture applied around the postpartum uterus to achieve mechanical tamponade and halt severe atonic postpartum haemorrhage.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Continuous surgical compression brace technique invented by Christopher B-Lynch to compress anterior and posterior myometrial walls together.
Uterus-preserving surgical alternative to bilateral hypogastric artery ligation or emergency peripartum hysterectomy.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Severe atonic postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) refractory to medical uterotonics (oxytocin, ergometrine, carboprost, misoprostol).
Low-lying placenta or placenta praevia with persistent lower uterine segment bleeding.
Morbidly adherent placenta managed conservatively with focal postpartum haemorrhage.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Patient positioned in Lloyd-Davies or lithotomy position with legs abducted to allow simultaneous vaginal observation of lochial flow.
Following caesarean delivery, reopen hysterotomy and exteriorise the uterus; following vaginal birth, perform rapid Pfannenstiel laparotomy and lower segment hysterotomy.
Test efficacy by performing vigorous bimanual uterine compression; cessation of vaginal haemorrhage confirms suitability for B-Lynch placement.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Select heavy absorbable synthetic suture (Vicryl No. 1 or Monocryl No. 1) mounted on a large curved round-bodied needle.
Puncture anterior uterine wall 3 cm below lower hysterotomy incision and 3 cm medial to the lateral border, entering the uterine cavity.
Direct needle out through the anterior wall 3 cm above the upper hysterotomy margin, keeping 4 cm medial to the cornual angle.
Carry the suture vertically over the uterine fundus (3 to 4 cm medial to the cornua) and down the posterior uterine wall.
Pierce posterior myometrium at the level of the hysterotomy, traverse the cavity horizontally, and exit the posterior wall contralaterally.
Loop suture vertically over the contralateral fundus and pass through anterior wall from above to below the hysterotomy.
Have an assistant exert firm two-handed fundal compression while the surgeon pulls both suture ends taut and knots them securely below the incision.
Inspect the cervix from below to verify patency and exclude entrapment, then close the hysterotomy and abdominal wall in layers.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Failure of hemostasis due to placenta percreta, delayed application, or severe consumptive coagulopathy (DIC).
Myometrial necrosis and uterine wall ischemia secondary to excessive suture tension.
Endocervical canal obliteration leading to postoperative haematometra, pyometra, or secondary Asherman syndrome.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Maintain in a high-dependency unit with continuous monitoring of vital parameters, urine output, and postpartum lochial discharge.
Continue intravenous uterotonic infusions for 24 hours to preserve intrinsic uterine tone.
Correct coagulopathy with fresh frozen plasma, platelets, and cryoprecipitate as clinically indicated.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Bimanual compression test is a mandatory prerequisite: If digital compression of the exteriorised uterus fails to stop bleeding, compression sutures will fail.
Modified techniques (Hayman suture) place 2 to 4 vertical transfixing sutures from anterior to posterior wall without opening the lower uterine segment, saving crucial minutes.
Pereira sutures place subserosal transverse and longitudinal bites; Cho square sutures create localized through-and-through compressive squares.

viva.q: What test must always be performed before applying a B-Lynch compression suture?
viva.a: Bimanual uterine compression test: The exteriorised uterus is firmly compressed between two hands. If vaginal bleeding visibly halts, B-Lynch suture application is indicated and likely to succeed.

viva.q: How does the Hayman compression technique differ from the classic B-Lynch suture?
viva.a: The Hayman suture passes straight through the anterior and posterior uterine walls from front to back without reopening the lower segment hysterotomy, saving time and avoiding suture line incision bleeding.

viva.q: What are the common causes of failure of B-Lynch compression sutures?
viva.a: Placenta percreta with deep myometrial invasion, delay in application after irreversible DIC has developed, overtightening causing tissue necrosis, and improper loose suture placement.

image.brief: Medical diagram of the uterus showing the B-Lynch compression brace suture pathway, looping over the fundus like suspenders and anchoring below the lower segment hysterotomy incision.

items.summary: Surgical stepwise vascular ligation of the ascending uterine and utero-ovarian arteries performed to arrest life-threatening atonic postpartum haemorrhage while preserving the uterus.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Bilateral operative devascularisation procedure described by O'Leary to arrest massive pelvic bleeding.
Conservative uterine-sparing surgical intervention that significantly reduces myometrial perfusion pressure while maintaining baseline tissue viability through pelvic collaterals.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Severe atonic postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) refractory to medical uterotonics.
Persistent lower uterine segment haemorrhage secondary to placenta praevia or morbidly adherent placenta.
Prophylactic pelvic vascular control during complex caesarean deliveries or reconstructive uterine operations.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Conducted under general or regional anaesthesia in supine or modified Lloyd-Davies position under strict operating room asepsis.
Ensure wide-bore intravenous lines, active transfusion of blood components, and exteriorisation of the uterus for optimal exposure.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Exteriorise the uterus and tilt it anteriorly and contralaterally to expose the broad ligament and lateral myometrial border.
Identify the ascending branch of the uterine artery running tortuously along the lateral uterine margin.
Pass a heavy absorbable suture (Vicryl No. 1 on a large curved needle) through the myometrium from anterior to posterior 2 to 3 cm medial to the vessels.
Direct the needle through the avascular window in the broad ligament and tie the ligature securely on the anterior myometrium, compressing ascending uterine vessels.
Repeat the identical ligation on the contralateral uterine artery.
If haemorrhage persists, perform utero-ovarian artery ligation by placing a deep myometrial transfixing ligature just below the utero-ovarian ligament insertion at the uterine cornu.
Proceed to low uterine artery ligation near the cervicovaginal junction if lower segment or vaginal angle bleeding continues.
Verify hemostasis across all pedicles, return the uterus into the pelvic cavity, and close the abdominal wall.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Iatrogenic ureteric injury, particularly when ligating low descending branches near the vaginal vault.
Broad ligament haematoma formation from inadvertent puncture of the accompanying uterine venous plexus.
Uterine necrosis or premature ovarian failure secondary to extensive vascular compromise (exceedingly rare).
Failure to arrest haemorrhage, necessitating internal iliac artery ligation or emergency peripartum hysterectomy.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Transfer to an intensive care unit for continuous hemodynamic, lochial flow, and urinary output monitoring.
Maintain maintenance uterotonic infusions and correct consumptive coagulopathy with appropriate blood components.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Stepwise uterine devascularisation succeeds in arresting over 80% of atonic PPH, avoiding radical peripartum hysterectomy.
The procedure cannot arrest bleeding from retained cotyledons, cervical tears, or active consumptive coagulopathy.
Future reproductive capability and normal menstruation are preserved due to extensive retroperitoneal pelvic anastomoses.

viva.q: What is the anatomical placement of the initial O'Leary uterine artery ligation stitch?
viva.a: The suture penetrates the anterior myometrium 2 to 3 cm below the lower segment hysterotomy, 2 to 3 cm medial to the lateral uterine margin, exits posteriorly, passes through an avascular broad ligament window, and knots anteriorly.

viva.q: What is the next surgical step if bilateral uterine artery ligation fails to halt atonic PPH?
viva.a: Perform bilateral utero-ovarian artery ligation just inferior to the insertion of the utero-ovarian ligaments at the cornua, followed if necessary by bilateral internal iliac artery ligation.

image.brief: Anatomical schematic showing the posterior view of the uterus with bilateral ligature sites marked on the ascending uterine arteries, utero-ovarian anastomosis, and descending vaginal branches.

items.summary: Bilateral ligation of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery to reduce pelvic pulse pressure and control intractable obstetric or gynaecological haemorrhage.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Surgical ligation of the internal iliac artery trunk or anterior branch to convert a high-pressure pulsatile pelvic arterial circuit into a low-pressure venous-like collateral network.
Reduces pelvic arterial pulse pressure by approximately 85%, promoting natural haemostatic thrombosis in bleeding pelvic viscera.

groups.label: Obstetric emergencies
bullets: Catastrophic atonic postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) failing medical therapy and compression sutures.
Severe haemorrhage from broad ligament haematomas, uterine rupture, or deep cervical-vaginal tears.
Major placenta praevia, placenta accreta spectrum, or placental abruption with Couvelaire uterus.

groups.label: Gynaecological and oncological uses
bullets: Uncontrolled pelvic haemorrhage during radical Wertheim hysterectomy or pelvic exenteration.
Intractable vaginal bleeding from advanced cervical or endometrial carcinoma.
Complex pelvic surgery involving severe endometriosis, dense pelvic adhesions, or large intraligamentary fibroids.
Prophylactic vascular control in Jehovah's Witness patients undergoing major pelvic resection.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Position patient supine with Trendelenburg tilt under general anaesthesia with large-volume blood products available.
Perform adequate midline vertical laparotomy to ensure clear visual exposure of the posterior pelvic peritoneum.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Pack bowel loops cephalad using moist laparotomy packs to expose the pelvic brim and sacroiliac articulation.
Palpate the common iliac artery pulsation and identify its bifurcation into external and internal iliac trunks.
Identify the ureter crossing the bifurcation of the common iliac artery on the medial leaf of the peritoneum.
Incise the posterior parietal peritoneum longitudinally lateral to the ureter and retract the ureter medially.
Dissect the perivascular sheath of the internal iliac artery gently using a blunt right-angled Mixter clamp.
Pass the Mixter clamp strictly from lateral to medial beneath the artery to protect the underlying external iliac vein.
Carry a heavy non-absorbable ligature (silk or prolene 1-0) beneath the vessel 2 to 3 cm distal to the bifurcation, preserving the posterior division.
Palpate the ipsilateral femoral artery in the groin to verify strong pulsations, confirming the external iliac artery is patent.
Tie the ligature firmly in continuity without transecting the vessel, and repeat the procedure on the opposite side.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Accidental ligation of the external iliac artery causing acute lower limb ischemia (cold, pale, pulseless leg).
Laceration of the internal or external iliac veins causing massive, difficult-to-control retroperitoneal hemorrhage.
Ureteric crush injury or transection resulting in urinoma or ureteroperitoneal fistula.
Ischaemic gluteal necrosis, pelvic nerve neuropraxia, spinal cord ischemia, or postoperative bladder atony.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Monitor peripheral pedal pulses, skin temperature, and capillary refill in both lower limbs continuously.
Retain indwelling urinary catheter to monitor renal function and manage transient neurogenic bladder atony.
Provide intensive care resuscitation with fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate, and packed red cells.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Always introduce the right-angled clamp from lateral to medial beneath the artery to avoid tearing the vulnerable external iliac vein.
Always confirm strong peripheral femoral pulsations prior to tying the ligature to rule out accidental external iliac occlusion.
Ligation is carried out 2 to 3 cm distal to the common iliac bifurcation to preserve the posterior division branch supplying gluteal musculature.

viva.q: What is the physiological mechanism by which internal iliac artery ligation controls pelvic haemorrhage?
viva.a: It converts the pelvic arterial circulation into a low-pressure venous-type system by reducing distal arterial pulse pressure by about 85%, allowing local clotting and hemostasis.

viva.q: Why must the right-angled Mixter forceps be passed from lateral to medial during dissection of the internal iliac artery?
viva.a: The external iliac vein lies immediately lateral and posterior to the internal iliac artery; passing the instrument from lateral to medial prevents blind tearing of this major thin-walled retroperitoneal vein.

viva.q: What vital physical examination check must be performed immediately prior to tying the hypogastric ligature?
viva.a: Palpate the ipsilateral femoral artery pulsation in the groin to confirm that the external iliac artery has not been inadvertently encircled.

image.brief: Surgical field illustration showing retroperitoneal exposure at the pelvic brim, showing bifurcation of common iliac artery, ureter retracted medially, and right-angled Mixter clamp passing beneath the internal iliac artery.

items.summary: Transabdominal surgical removal of the uterine corpus and cervix with or without bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy via an open laparotomy incision.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Complete surgical excision of the uterus including the cervix through an abdominal wall incision.
May be performed with preservation of the adnexa or combined with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (BSO) based on patient age and pathology.

groups.label: Gynaecological indications
bullets: Large symptomatic uterine leiomyomas, adenomyosis, or severe refractory endometriosis.
Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) unresponsive to medical management.
Premalignant and malignant lesions: Endometrial hyperplasia with atypia, early cervical carcinoma (stage Ia1), endometrial cancer, ovarian malignancy, or gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.

groups.label: Obstetric emergency indications
bullets: Catastrophic atonic postpartum haemorrhage refractory to medical and conservative surgical interventions.
Morbidly adherent placenta (placenta accreta spectrum) with extensive myometrial invasion.
Extensive uterine rupture beyond surgical reconstruction, or severe septic abortion.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Patient placed supine under general or regional anaesthesia with empty bladder via Foley catheter drainage.
Prepare abdominal wall and vagina under strict surgical asepsis, draping widely for potential midline extension.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Enter peritoneal cavity through a lower transverse or midline vertical laparotomy incision and pack bowel cephalad.

Apply first set of clamps: If conserving ovaries, clamp round ligament, fallopian tube near cornu, and ovarian ligament; if removing ovaries (BSO), clamp round ligament and infundibulopelvic ligament.
Divide and transfix clamped pedicles securely with absorbable sutures (Vicryl No. 1) bilaterally.
Incise the uterovesical peritoneal fold transversely and mobilise the urinary bladder inferiorly off the cervix using gauze dissection.
Apply second set of clamps: Place heavy curved clamps across uterine vessels at the level of the internal os flush with the myometrium, divide, and transfix with Vicryl No. 1.
Apply third set of clamps: Clamp the Mackenrodt (cardinal) and uterosacral ligaments close to the lateral cervix, divide, and transfix.
Incise the anterior vaginal vault below the cervix, circumcise the vaginal cuff, and deliver the uterus and cervix intact.
Close the vaginal vault with continuous or interrupted absorbable sutures, anchoring the cardinal and uterosacral stumps to the angles to prevent vault prolapse.
Verify meticulous haemostasis across all retroperitoneal pedicles, confirm sponge and instrument counts, and close the abdominal wall.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Iatrogenic ureteric injury occurring at the infundibulopelvic ligament, uterine artery crossing, or vaginal vault angles.
Accidental bladder laceration during vesicouterine plane dissection, or secondary bowel injury.
Pelvic haematoma, vault cellulitis, pelvic abscess, and wound infection.
Deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism, paralytic ileus, and acute urinary retention.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Maintain indwelling Foley catheter for 24 hours and record urine output hourly.
Provide scheduled multimodal analgesia, thromboprophylaxis with LMWH, and encourage early ambulation.
Advise abstinence from vaginal intercourse and avoidance of strenuous physical lifting for 6 weeks.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Always clamp uterine vessels perpendicularly flush against the lateral uterine border to keep well clear of the descending ureter ('water under the bridge').
Incorporation of Mackenrodt and uterosacral ligament stumps into the lateral vaginal vault closure is essential to maintain apex suspension and prevent future vault prolapse.

viva.q: What structures are clamped in the first set of pedicles during total abdominal hysterectomy with conservation of ovaries?
viva.a: The round ligament, the fallopian tube close to the uterine cornu, and the utero-ovarian ligament. If ovaries are removed (BSO), the infundibulopelvic ligament is clamped instead of the adnexal pedicle.

viva.q: Where is the ureter most vulnerable to iatrogenic injury during abdominal hysterectomy?
viva.a: At three critical points: where it crosses beneath the infundibulopelvic ligament at the pelvic brim, where it passes under the uterine artery 1.5 cm lateral to the cervix, and at the lateral vaginal vault angle.

viva.q: Why are the uterosacral and cardinal ligaments anchored to the vaginal vault during closure?
viva.a: To provide robust apical support to the vaginal vault, reconstructing the normal endopelvic fascial framework and preventing subsequent vaginal vault prolapse.

image.brief: Medical surgical diagram of total abdominal hysterectomy showing the three successive clamping levels: cornual or infundibulopelvic pedicle, uterine artery at the internal os, and Mackenrodt and uterosacral ligaments.

items.summary: Transvaginal reconstructive surgery to repair anterior vaginal wall laxity and herniation of the urinary bladder (cystocele) by plicating the pubocervical fascia.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Surgical reconstruction of the anterior vaginal compartment to correct a cystocele or cystourethrocele.
Restores normal pelvic anatomy by reducing bladder herniation, plicating attenuated pubocervical fibromuscular tissue, and resecting redundant vaginal epithelium.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Symptomatic cystocele causing pelvic heaviness, vaginal bulging, or dragging discomfort.
Cystourethrocele associated with voiding dysfunction, urinary frequency, or incomplete bladder evacuation.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Placed in dorsal lithotomy position under regional or general anaesthesia with full surgical asepsis.
Catheterise to empty bladder; administer perioperative intravenous prophylactic antibiotics.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Retract the posterior vaginal wall with a Sims speculum and grasp the anterior cervical lip with a vulsellum or tenaculum to apply traction.
Insert a metallic catheter into the urethra to palpate the bladder neck and establish the lower border of the bladder reflection.
Make a transverse incision at the vesicocervical junction and a vertical midline incision extending superiorly to 1 to 2 cm below the external urethral meatus, forming an inverted-T.
Dissect the subepithelial plane laterally on each side, separating vaginal mucosa off the pubocervical fascia and bladder muscularis.
Divide the vesicocervical ligament and mobilise the bladder base superiorly off the anterior cervical surface.
Plicate the pubocervical fascia across the midline over the bladder base using interrupted or purse-string absorbable sutures (Vicryl No. 1 or 0) to buttress the cystocele.
Trim redundant lateral vaginal epithelial flaps conservatively to avoid excessive vaginal narrowing.
Close the anterior vaginal mucosa with interrupted or continuous locking absorbable sutures (Vicryl 1 or 2-0).
Insert an indwelling Foley catheter and pack the vagina lightly with antiseptic gauze.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Intraoperative cystotomy (bladder perforation) or heavy venous plexus haemorrhage.
Postoperative urinary retention, urinary tract infection, or de novo stress urinary incontinence.
Late complications including vesicovaginal fistula, vaginal stenosis, dyspareunia, or cystocele recurrence.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Maintain indwelling Foley catheter drainage for 24 to 48 hours to protect fascial plication lines.
Remove vaginal gauze pack after 24 hours and ensure spontaneous voiding after catheter trial.
Advise avoidance of heavy lifting, chronic straining, and vaginal intercourse for 6 weeks.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Careful dissection in the true avascular subepithelial plane between vaginal mucosa and pubocervical fascia minimizes blood loss and preserves fascial tissue for plication.
If cystotomy occurs, recognize it immediately, repair in two layers with absorbable sutures, and maintain continuous urinary catheter drainage for 7 to 10 days.

viva.q: What is the primary supportive tissue layer plicated during anterior colporrhaphy?
viva.a: The pubocervical fascia (endopelvic fibromuscular layer), which extends from the pubic bones to the cervix and supports the bladder base and urethra.

viva.q: Why is a metal catheter inserted during the initial steps of anterior colporrhaphy?
viva.a: To locate the bladder neck and identify the lowest extent of the bladder reflection, ensuring the transverse mucosal incision is placed safely below the bladder margin.

image.brief: Transvaginal surgical illustration of anterior colporrhaphy showing inverted-T incision, lateral reflection of vaginal mucosal flaps, and midline plication of pubocervical fascia over the bladder.

items.summary: Transvaginal reconstructive procedure to repair rectocele and restore the perineal body by plicating rectovaginal fascia and re-approximating the levator ani muscles.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Reconstructive vaginal procedure to correct herniation of the rectum into the posterior vaginal canal (rectocele).
Frequently combined with perineorrhaphy (colpoperineorrhaphy) to reconstruct an attenuated perineal body and narrow a gaping vaginal introitus.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Symptomatic rectocele presenting with vaginal bulge, pelvic dragging, or defaecatory dysfunction requiring digital vaginal splinting.
Perineal body deficiency and gaping genital hiatus following obstetric perineal trauma.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Patient in lithotomy position under regional or general anaesthesia with perineal and rectal skin asepsis.
Infiltrate submucosal plane with saline or 0.5% bupivacaine with 1:200,000 adrenaline to facilitate hydrodissection and reduce bleeding.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Place two Allis forceps at the level of the introitus on the carunculae myrtiformes and a third at the apex of the rectocele.
Make a transverse incision across the posterior fourchette between the introital Allis forceps.
Extend a vertical incision from the midpoint of the horizontal cut superiorly to the rectocele apex, delineating a triangular flap.
Dissect the posterior vaginal mucosa laterally in the subepithelial plane, separating it off the underlying rectovaginal septum and rectum.
Reduce the rectocele and plicate the rectovaginal (pararectal) fascia over the anterior rectal wall using interrupted or purse-string absorbable sutures (Vicryl No. 1 or 0).
Approximate the medial bellies of the levator ani muscles (puborectalis) across the midline with 1 to 2 interrupted absorbable sutures to reconstruct the perineal shelf.
Excise redundant triangular posterior vaginal mucosal flaps conservatively.
Close the posterior vaginal epithelium with continuous or interrupted Vicryl sutures, and reconstruct the superficial perineal muscles and skin in layers.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Accidental intraoperative rectal perforation or posterior wall haemorrhage.
Postoperative urinary retention, pelvic haematoma, or perineal wound dehiscence.
Late dyspareunia from over-tightening of the introitus, rectovaginal fistula, or faecal and flatus incontinence.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Prescribe stool softeners and high-fibre diet to prevent straining and protect the rectovaginal suture line.
Remove vaginal pack after 24 hours and maintain good perineal hygiene with warm sitz baths.
Instruct patient to avoid intercourse and heavy lifting for 6 weeks.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Always perform digital rectal examination at the conclusion of the surgery to ensure that no plication sutures have inadvertently breached the rectal mucosa.
Overzealous approximation of levator ani muscles high up causes severe, intractable introital dyspareunia; repair must focus primarily on rectovaginal fascial plication.

viva.q: What mandatory examination step must be performed at the end of posterior colporrhaphy?
viva.a: A digital rectal examination must be carried out to verify rectal wall integrity and ensure that no sutures have penetrated through the rectal mucosa into the rectal lumen.

viva.q: What are the components of colpoperineorrhaphy?
viva.a: Posterior colporrhaphy (plication of rectovaginal fascia over the rectum) combined with perineorrhaphy (approximation of levator ani muscles, superficial perineal muscles, and perineal skin closure).

image.brief: Surgical diagram of posterior colporrhaphy illustrating triangular posterior vaginal flap dissection, midline plication of rectovaginal fascia over the rectum, and levator ani muscle approximation.

items.summary: Surgical obliteration of the herniation sac of the pouch of Douglas and reconstruction of the vaginal apex via vaginal or abdominal culdoplasty.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: True peritoneal herniation through the upper third of the posterior vaginal wall containing small bowel or omentum.
Repaired through transvaginal high sac ligation and culdoplasty (McCall) or transabdominal obliterative procedures (Moschcowitz or Halban).

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Symptomatic enterocele manifesting as an apex bulge or herniation of the pouch of Douglas.
Post-hysterectomy vaginal vault prolapse associated with enterocele sac formation.
Prophylactic obliteration of a deep cul-de-sac during vaginal hysterectomy.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Lithotomy position for transvaginal repair or supine with Trendelenburg tilt for transabdominal surgery under general or regional anaesthesia.
Ensure complete bladder and bowel evacuation with standard surgical draping and antisepsis.

groups.label: Vaginal approaches
bullets: Dissect enterocele sac free from the posterior vaginal wall up to its neck at the level of the uterosacral ligaments.
Place high purse-string non-absorbable sutures around the peritoneal sac neck, incorporating the uterosacral ligaments, and excise redundant peritoneum.
Suspend the vaginal cuff to the cardinal-uterosacral ligament complex.
Internal McCall culdoplasty: Anchor suture through one uterosacral ligament, weave through highest cul-de-sac peritoneum, and exit through the opposite uterosacral ligament.
External McCall culdoplasty: Pass suture through full-thickness posterior vaginal wall, ipsilateral uterosacral ligament, peritoneum, and opposite structures, tying inside the vagina.

groups.label: Abdominal approaches
bullets: Moschcowitz operation: Place concentric circular purse-string sutures from the bottom of the cul-de-sac upward, catching pelvic peritoneum, vaginal vault, and anterior rectal serosa.
Halban operation: Apply vertical longitudinal sutures approximating the anterior rectal wall serosa to the posterior vaginal wall and pelvic peritoneum.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Accidental kinking, entrapment, or transfixion of the ureters during high uterosacral or peritoneal suturing.
Rectal laceration or perforation during deep cul-de-sac dissection.
Haemorrhage from presacral or pararectal venous plexuses.
Recurrent vault prolapse or enterocele recurrence.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Maintain urinary catheterization and stool softeners to avoid postoperative straining.
Advise avoidance of heavy lifting and sexual intercourse for 6 weeks.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: McCall culdoplasty is the procedure of choice during vaginal hysterectomy, effectively closing the cul-de-sac and preventing secondary enterocele.
Care must be taken to identify ureteric courses laterally before placing deep bites through the uterosacral ligaments.

viva.q: What is the anatomical difference between an internal and external McCall culdoplasty?
viva.a: Internal McCall places sutures exclusively through the uterosacral ligaments and high cul-de-sac peritoneum, whereas external McCall incorporates the full thickness of the posterior vaginal wall, tying knots inside the vagina.

viva.q: Which major structure is at greatest risk of iatrogenic entrapment during high enterocele repair?
viva.a: The ureters, which course anterolateral to the uterosacral ligaments near the ischial spines and can be kinked or ligated by lateral suture placement.

image.brief: Diagram of McCall culdoplasty illustrating high purse-string suture passing through bilateral uterosacral ligaments and cul-de-sac peritoneum to obliterate the enterocele space.

items.summary: Transvaginal surgical removal of the uterus and cervix without an abdominal incision, indicated for uterovaginal prolapse and select benign uterine pathologies.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Surgical excision of the entire uterus and cervix accomplished completely through the vaginal route.
Primary surgical approach for uterine prolapse, associated with less postoperative pain, quicker recovery, and absence of abdominal scars.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Uterovaginal prolapse (second-degree or third-degree uterine descent).
Benign abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) refractory to medical treatment in a mobile uterus.
Small uterine leiomyomas (uterine size less than 12 weeks gestation) with pelvic floor descent.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Patient in steep lithotomy position under regional or general anaesthesia with bladder drained.
Strict surgical asepsis of the perineum, vagina, and surrounding operative field.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Retract posterior vaginal wall with a Sims speculum and grasp anterior and posterior cervical lips with vulsellum forceps.
Infiltrate cervicovaginal junction with saline or dilute vasopressin/adrenaline solution to establish hydrodissection.
Make a circumferential incision around the cervix at the cervicovaginal junction.
Push the bladder upward off the anterior cervix to enter the anterior uterovesical pouch.
Enter the pouch of Douglas sharply posteriorly and insert a weighted Auvard speculum into the peritoneal cavity.
Apply first set of clamps to uterosacral and Mackenrodt (cardinal) ligaments, divide, and transfix with Vicryl No. 1.
Apply second set of clamps to the uterine vessels flush against the lower uterine body, divide, and transfix bilaterally.
Deliver the uterine fundus either posteriorly or anteriorly using Doderlein manoeuvre.
Apply third set of clamps across the cornual pedicles (round ligament, fallopian tube, ovarian ligament), divide, and transfix securely.
Inspect all vascular pedicles for haemostasis and extraperitonealise the stumps.
Perform anterior and posterior pelvic floor repair (Ward-Mayo procedure) if cystocele or rectocele is present.
Close the vaginal vault securely, anchoring the cardinal and uterosacral ligament pedicles to the lateral vault angles.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Intraoperative haemorrhage or pedicle slippage into the peritoneal cavity.
Iatrogenic cystotomy, ureteric transection, or rectal trauma.
Pelvic haematoma, vault cellulitis, or pelvic abscess formation.
Postoperative deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism, urinary retention, and late vault prolapse.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Remove vaginal gauze pack after 24 hours and maintain Foley catheter for 24 hours.
Encourage early ambulation and provide scheduled analgesia and thromboprophylaxis.
Instruct patient to avoid sexual intercourse and heavy physical exertion for 6 weeks.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Clamping order in vaginal hysterectomy is the exact reverse of abdominal hysterectomy: Uterosacral/cardinal first, uterine vessels second, and cornual pedicles last.
Contraindicated in fixed, immobile uteri (severe pelvic endometriosis, pelvic inflammatory disease), suspected pelvic malignancy, or excessively enlarged uteri.

viva.q: What is the sequence of clamping during a vaginal hysterectomy?
viva.a: First set: Uterosacral and Mackenrodt (cardinal) ligaments. Second set: Uterine blood vessels. Third set: Cornual structures comprising the round ligament, fallopian tube, and ovarian ligament.

viva.q: What is the Doderlein manoeuvre during vaginal hysterectomy?
viva.a: A surgical technique where the uterine fundus is hooked and exteriorised through the posterior pouch of Douglas or anterior uterovesical space, converting the final cornual pedicles into an accessible position.

image.brief: Surgical diagram of vaginal hysterectomy showing circumferential cervical incision, opening of the posterior pouch of Douglas, and clamping of the uterosacral and cardinal ligament complex.

items.summary: En bloc resection of the uterus, cervix, parametrium, paracolpos, upper vaginal cuff, and pelvic lymph nodes for early-stage cervical carcinoma.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Extensive oncological procedure for invasive cervical cancer (stages Ib1 to IIa) and select stage II endometrial carcinomas.
Involves wide en bloc excision of the uterus, adnexa, broad ligament parametria to pelvic sidewalls, upper third to half of vagina, and regional pelvic lymphadenectomy.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Carcinoma of the cervix stage Ib1, Ib2, and IIa1.
Carcinoma of the endometrium with cervical stromal invasion (stage II).
Rarely, clear cell adenocarcinoma of the cervix or vagina in young women.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Conducted under general anaesthesia with supine lithotomy positioning and prophylactic vaginal iodine packing.
Prepare blood products and maintain continuous arterial line and central venous monitoring.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Open abdomen through a generous midline vertical incision from symphysis pubis to above the umbilicus.
Explore the peritoneal cavity thoroughly, palpating the liver, diaphragm, omentum, and para-aortic lymph nodes to exclude distant metastases.
Divide and transfix round ligaments bilaterally and open the broad ligament leaves.
Develop the paravesical and pararectal avascular retroperitoneal spaces by blunt and sharp dissection.
Dissect and ligate the infundibulopelvic ligaments bilaterally (if ovaries are to be resected).
Identify the ureter in the retroperitoneum and trace it through the ureteric tunnel beneath the uterine artery.
Dissect and ligate the uterine artery at its origin from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery.
Unroof the ureter completely from the vesicouterine ligament, mobilising the bladder base well below the upper vagina.
Resect the uterosacral ligaments near their sacral attachments and cardinal ligaments at the pelvic sidewall.
Excise an upper vaginal cuff of 3 to 4 cm and remove the specimen en bloc.
Perform systematic pelvic lymphadenectomy including external iliac, internal iliac, common iliac, and obturator lymph nodes.
Close the vaginal cuff, confirm meticulous retroperitoneal hemostasis, and place closed-suction pelvic drains.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Major intraoperative haemorrhage from pelvic venous plexuses or internal iliac branches.
Iatrogenic ureteric transection, devascularisation, or ureterovaginal fistula formation.
Bladder atony and denervation requiring prolonged indwelling urinary catheterisation for weeks.
Pelvic lymphocele, lower limb lymphedema, deep vein thrombosis, and pulmonary embolism.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Maintain indwelling Foley catheter for 7 to 14 days and check post-void residual volumes before discharge.
Administer extended postoperative pharmacological thromboprophylaxis with LMWH for 4 weeks.
Monitor retroperitoneal pelvic drain output until drainage is less than 30 to 50 mL in 24 hours.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: In Piver-Rutledge Type I (extrafascial), parametria are not resected; in Type II (Wertheim), uterine arteries are tied where crossing the ureter; in Type III (Meigs), uterine arteries are tied at their hypogastric origin.

Dissection of the paravesical space (bounded by obliterated umbilical artery, bladder, and obturator internus) and pararectal space (between internal iliac and rectum) is the foundation of radical pelvic dissection.

viva.q: What are the anatomical boundaries of the parametrial excision in a Type III (Meigs) radical hysterectomy?
viva.a: Uterine artery ligated at its origin from the anterior division of internal iliac artery, uterosacral ligaments resected at their sacral insertion, cardinal ligaments divided flush at the pelvic sidewall, and upper half of vagina resected.

viva.q: Why is prolonged bladder catheterisation required following radical hysterectomy?
viva.a: Extensive dissection of the cardinal and uterosacral ligaments disrupts parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4), causing temporary autonomic bladder denervation and detrusor atony.

viva.q: What retroperitoneal spaces must be developed to perform pelvic lymphadenectomy and parametrial dissection?
viva.a: The paravesical space anteriorly and the pararectal space posteriorly, separated by the cardinal ligament (Mackenrodt ligament) containing the uterine artery and ureter.

image.brief: Pelvic anatomical diagram showing radical hysterectomy dissection planes, illustrating unroofed ureter traversing the ureteric canal, uterine artery ligated at internal iliac origin, and pelvic lymph node stations.

items.summary: Surgical enucleation and excision of uterine leiomyomas with anatomical reconstruction of the uterine wall, indicated for fertility conservation.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Operative enucleation of benign uterine fibroids (leiomyomas) with anatomical myometrial reconstruction.
Procedure of choice for symptomatic leiomyomas in women wishing to preserve future fertility or maintain uterine integrity.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Symptomatic fibroids in nulliparous women or patients desiring future childbearing.
Recurrent pregnancy loss or infertility attributable to cavity-distorting submucous or intramural myomas.
Pelvic pressure symptoms, severe dysmenorrhoea, or menorrhagia in patients desiring uterine conservation.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Preoperative anaemia correction using oral or parenteral iron, blood transfusions, and gonadotrophin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists for 3 to 6 months to reduce fibroid volume.
Conducted under regional or general anaesthesia in supine position with indwelling urinary catheter.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Enter abdomen through a transverse or midline incision and apply temporary vascular control measures.
Inject dilute vasopressin (20 units in 50 mL normal saline) into the myometrium surrounding the myoma capsule to produce vasoconstriction.
Apply Bonney myomectomy clamp or a soft rubber tourniquet around the uterine isthmus to occlude uterine vessels temporarily.
Make a single anterior vertical or transverse uterine incision over the pseudocapsule of the most prominent fibroid.
Incise the pseudocapsule cleanly and grasp the fibroid with a tenaculum or single-toothed vulsellum.
Enucleate the fibroid from its myometrial bed using blunt and sharp dissection while taking care not to breach the endometrial cavity.
Enucleate secondary myomas through the primary incision wherever technically feasible to minimize serosal scarring.
Obliterate the myoma bed dead space in multiple layers using interrupted absorbable sutures (Vicryl No. 1 or 0).
Close the overlying uterine serosa cleanly with baseball or continuous subserosal Vicryl sutures, and release vascular tourniquets.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Severe intraoperative haemorrhage necessitating emergency conversion to peripartum or total hysterectomy.
Iatrogenic entry into the endometrial cavity, increasing the risk of postoperative intrauterine synechiae.
Postoperative pelvic adhesions causing secondary tubal factor subfertility.
Uterine scar rupture during subsequent pregnancy or labour.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Monitor hemoglobin and hematocrit postoperatively and manage pain with scheduled multimodal analgesia.
Advise delaying conception for 3 to 6 months to allow adequate myometrial tensile wound healing.
