Recommend elective caesarean delivery in future pregnancies if the myometrial cavity was breached or extensive dissection performed.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Minimise incisions: A single anterior uterine incision used to extract multiple fibroids reduces subsequent peritoneal adhesions.
Bonney hood operation: Technique for large fundal or posterior fibroids where a transverse incision is made and the posterior myometrial flap is sutured forward over the fundus as a protective hood.

viva.q: What intraoperative pharmacologic and mechanical techniques are used to minimize blood loss during myomectomy?
viva.a: Intramyometrial infiltration of dilute vasopressin (20 units in 50 mL saline), mechanical pericervical tourniquet or Bonney myomectomy clamp, and atraumatic vascular clamps on the infundibulopelvic vessels.

viva.q: What is the surgical significance of breaching the endometrial cavity during myomectomy?
viva.a: Breaching the endometrium increases postoperative intrauterine synechiae formation (Asherman syndrome), postoperative menorrhagia, and mandates elective caesarean delivery in future pregnancies to avoid uterine rupture.

image.brief: Surgical operative illustration of myomectomy showing single midline anterior uterine incision, tenaculum grasping the enucleated fibroid from its pseudocapsule bed, and tourniquet around the lower uterine segment.

items.summary: Catheter-directed interventional radiological embolisation of bilateral uterine arteries to devascularise symptomatic leiomyomas or control refractory pelvic haemorrhage.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Minimally invasive endovascular procedure performed under fluoroscopic guidance by an interventional radiologist.
Selectively introduces calibrated particulate embolic agents into both uterine arteries to produce ischemic infarction and shrinkage of leiomyomas while preserving normal myometrium.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Symptomatic uterine leiomyomas causing menorrhagia, dysmenorrhoea, or bulk symptoms in women wishing to avoid surgery.
Failed medical management of abnormal uterine bleeding with completed family.
Acute or recurrent intractable postpartum haemorrhage or post-surgical pelvic bleeding refractory to conservative therapy.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Patient in supine position on the fluoroscopy table under local anaesthesia with conscious sedation.
Ensure sterile preparation of groin, adequate pre-procedural hydration, and prophylactic antiemetics and analgesics.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Puncture common femoral artery under ultrasound guidance using the Seldinger technique and insert an arterial sheath.
Advance a guidewire and selective catheter through the external iliac into the internal iliac artery under fluoroscopic guidance.
Cannulate the anterior division and selectively engage the main trunk of the uterine artery.
Inject radiopaque iodinated contrast medium to perform angiographic roadmapping and confirm catheter placement.
Infuse calibrated particulate embolic material (polyvinyl alcohol particles or gelatin microspheres) slowly until arterial sluggishness and stasis are achieved.
Withdraw the catheter, cross the aortic bifurcation, and perform selective embolisation of the contralateral uterine artery.
Remove vascular sheath and achieve groin hemostasis using manual compression or an endovascular vascular closure device.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Post-embolisation syndrome: Self-limiting fever, severe cramping pelvic pain, nausea, vomiting, and malaise occurring within 2 weeks.
Femoral puncture site haematoma, pseudoaneurysm, or contrast-induced allergic reaction.
Non-target embolisation into the ovarian artery leading to ovarian infarction, premature ovarian failure, or amenorrhoea.
Transcervical expulsion or vaginal sloughing of necrotic submucous fibroids, occasionally causing endometritis or sepsis requiring emergency hysterectomy.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Maintain strict bed rest with femoral puncture leg extended for 4 to 6 hours.
Provide aggressive scheduled analgesia with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and patient-controlled opioid analgesia.
Monitor for vaginal discharge, fever, or pain indicative of fibroid sloughing or secondary infection.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Clinical success rate is 80% to 90%, with an average fibroid volume reduction of 40% to 80% over 6 to 12 months.
Absolute contraindications include viable pregnancy, active pelvic sepsis, suspected pelvic genital tract malignancy, and refusal of potential hysterectomy.

viva.q: What is post-embolisation syndrome following uterine artery embolisation?
viva.a: A common constellation of acute ischemic pelvic pain, low-grade pyrexia, nausea, vomiting, leukocytosis, and malaise occurring within 48 hours to 2 weeks post-procedure, managed with analgesics and anti-inflammatories.

viva.q: What are the absolute contraindications to uterine artery embolisation?
viva.a: Active pregnancy, active or recent pelvic inflammatory disease/sepsis, suspected genital tract malignancy, and patient unwillingness to accept emergency hysterectomy if severe complications occur.

image.brief: Fluoroscopic pelvic angiogram diagram showing catheter introduced via femoral artery navigating into the tortuous uterine artery, demonstrating contrast distribution into fibroid hypervascular capillary network.

items.summary: Surgical enucleation and excision of a benign ovarian cyst with preservation of functional residual ovarian cortex and follicular reserve.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Surgical stripping and excision of a benign ovarian cyst wall while conserving the surrounding ovarian stroma and cortex.
Standard fertility-preserving procedure for benign ovarian neoplasms in reproductive-aged women, performed laparoscopically or via open laparotomy.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Persistent or symptomatic benign ovarian cysts: Dermoid cysts (mature cystic teratomas), endometriomas, and benign serous or mucinous cystadenomas.
Ovarian cysts exceeding 5 cm in diameter or failing to resolve spontaneously over 2 to 3 menstrual cycles.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Conducted under general anaesthesia in supine or Trendelenburg lithotomy position with empty bladder.
Review preoperative ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and tumor markers (CA-125) to confirm benign features prior to surgery.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Access pelvic cavity laparoscopically or via a small Pfannenstiel laparotomy incision.
Mobilise the ovary gently using atraumatic instruments and inspect the entire pelvic cavity.
Make a shallow, superficial elliptical incision over the thinnest portion of the antimesenteric ovarian cortex down to the cyst wall.
Identify the cleavage plane between the white cyst capsule and the vascular ovarian cortical tissue.
Dissect the cyst capsule circumferentially using gentle traction and counter-traction with blunt and sharp dissection without puncturing the cyst.
If performing laparoscopically, place the intact cyst into an impermeable endobag before decompressive aspiration and extraction through the port site.
Achieve meticulous hemostasis in the remaining ovarian bed using fine bipolar cautery or fine absorbable sutures.
Obliterate the dead space and reconstitute normal ovarian architecture by re-approximating the cortex with fine inverted absorbable sutures (Vicryl 3-0 or 4-0).

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Accidental intraoperative cyst rupture and peritoneal spillage (chemical peritonitis from dermoid contents, dense adhesions from endometrioma).
Ovarian stromal damage or excessive thermal injury reducing ovarian follicular reserve.
Postoperative ovarian bed haematoma, pelvic adhesion formation, and late recurrence of the cyst.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Provide scheduled analgesia and discharge day-care laparoscopic patients within 24 hours.
Advise early mobilization and send all excised cyst specimens for definitive histopathological evaluation.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Spillage of dermoid contents (sebaceous material and hair) causes severe chemical peritonitis; if rupture occurs, perform copious warm saline peritoneal lavage.
Spillage of an unsuspected ovarian malignancy upstages the tumor from Stage Ia to Stage Ic, drastically worsening oncological prognosis.

viva.q: Why is accidental intraoperative rupture of a dermoid cyst hazardous, and how is it managed?
viva.a: Dermoid cyst contents cause severe chemical granulomatous peritonitis. If accidental rupture occurs, immediately place the cyst into an endobag and perform copious warm saline peritoneal lavage until clear.

viva.q: How does intraoperative spillage impact the staging of an unsuspected malignant ovarian tumor?
viva.a: Accidental intraoperative capsule rupture of a malignant ovarian neoplasm automatically upstages an encapsulated Stage Ia tumor to Stage Ic1, requiring adjuvant platinum-based chemotherapy.

image.brief: Medical illustration of ovarian cystectomy showing elliptical cortical incision over the ovary and gentle traction separating the intact white cyst wall from the surrounding ovarian parenchyma.

items.summary: Operative surgical management of tubal ectopic gestation via laparoscopic or open salpingectomy, partial tubal resection, or conservative linear salpingotomy.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Emergency surgical treatment for ectopic gestations implanted outside the endometrial cavity, primarily within the fallopian tube.
Comprises radical procedures (total or partial salpingectomy) and conservative organ-preserving operations (linear salpingotomy or salpingostomy).

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Ruptured tubal ectopic gestation presenting with acute hemoperitoneum and hemodynamic compromise.
Unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy unsuitable for or failing medical therapy with methotrexate.
Salpingotomy indicated in unruptured ampullary ectopic pregnancy when the contralateral tube is absent or damaged and future fertility is desired.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Supine lithotomy position under general endotracheal anaesthesia with rapid vascular access.
Ensure availability of cross-matched packed red cells and prepare abdomen under strict surgical asepsis.

groups.label: Total salpingectomy
bullets: Grasp the fallopian tube with atraumatic forceps to elevate the mesosalpinx.
Progressively coagulate and divide the mesosalpinx close to the tube from the fimbrial end towards the cornual junction.
Ligate or excise the tube cleanly at the cornual angle and extract the specimen in an endobag.

groups.label: Partial salpingectomy
bullets: Apply clamps on either side of the gestational sac on the fallopian tube.
Perform segmental resection of the involved tubal segment and securely ligate both cut ends.

groups.label: Linear salpingotomy and salpingostomy
bullets: Make a 1 to 2 cm longitudinal incision along the antimesenteric border over the most prominent ectopic bulge.
Evacuate conceptive products gently using hydrodissection and suction without scraping the delicate tubal endosalpinx.
Achieve meticulous hemostasis of the tubal bed using fine microbipolar electrocautery.
In salpingotomy, close the incision with fine absorbable sutures; in salpingostomy, leave edges open to heal by secondary intention.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Intraoperative haemorrhage from the mesosalpingeal vascular arcade.
Persistent trophoblastic tissue following salpingotomy requiring systemic methotrexate therapy.
Recurrent ectopic pregnancy in the conserved tube or pelvic adhesion formation.
Secondary infertility or loss of tubal transport architecture.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Monitor maternal hemoglobin and administer Rh anti-D immunoglobulin to unsensitised Rh-negative patients.
For conservative salpingotomy, perform serial weekly serum beta-hCG measurements until levels drop below 5 mIU/mL.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Fimbriectomy involves excision of the infundibulum and fimbriae, precluding spontaneous tubal ovum pickup.
Milking the fallopian tube (expressing gestation from ampulla through fimbrial ostium) carries high persistent trophoblast rates and is discouraged.

viva.q: What is the key surgical difference between salpingotomy and salpingostomy?
viva.a: In salpingotomy, the linear tubal antimesenteric incision is closed using fine absorbable sutures, whereas in salpingostomy the tubal incision is left open to heal spontaneously by secondary intention.

viva.q: Why is serial beta-hCG monitoring mandatory following conservative surgical salpingotomy?
viva.a: To detect persistent ectopic trophoblastic tissue retained in the tubal wall, which occurs in 5% to 15% of cases and requires treatment with systemic methotrexate.

image.brief: Surgical diagram of fallopian tube ectopic pregnancy illustrating linear antimesenteric incision, gentle hydrodissection of gestational sac, and mesosalpingeal vascular anatomy.

title.en: Repair of Third- and Fourth-Degree Perineal Tears

items.summary: Systematic surgical reconstruction of obstetric anal sphincter injuries (OASIS) involving the external and internal anal sphincters and rectal mucosa.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Surgical repair of severe obstetric perineal trauma classified into third-degree (anal sphincter complex involvement) and fourth-degree (breach of rectal mucosa).
Essential reconstruction to preserve anal continence, prevent rectovaginal fistula formation, and restore the perineal body.

groups.label: Tear classification
bullets: Third-degree 3a: Partial tear of external anal sphincter (EAS) involving less than 50% of muscle thickness.
Third-degree 3b: Tear involving more than 50% of the external anal sphincter thickness.
Third-degree 3c: Complete tear of both external anal sphincter and internal anal sphincter (IAS) with intact rectal mucosa.
Fourth-degree tear: Complete disruption of perineal body, EAS, IAS, and the anorectal epithelium.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Patient in lithotomy position under regional (spinal or epidural) or general anaesthesia with good overhead illumination.
Perform systematic bimanual and digital rectal examination to determine the apex and depth of sphincter disruption.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Repair the rectal mucosa in fourth-degree tears using fine absorbable suture (PDS or Vicryl 2-0 or 3-0) with interrupted or continuous submucosal stitches.
Identify the internal anal sphincter (IAS) appearing as a glistening, pale fibrous muscle sheet between rectal mucosa and EAS.
Approximate the internal anal sphincter with interrupted or horizontal mattress sutures using 2-0 or 3-0 PDS or Vicryl.
Identify the retracted fibrous ends of the external anal sphincter (EAS) with Allis forceps.
Reconstruct the EAS using either an end-to-end approximation or an overlapping technique using 2-0 PDS or Vicryl sutures.
Place an anchoring suture 1 cm above the vaginal laceration apex and close the vaginal mucosa and rectovaginal fascia with continuous rapid-absorbing suture (Vicryl Rapide).
Approximate the deep and superficial transverse perineal muscles with interrupted sutures to rebuild the perineal body.
Close the perineal skin with subcuticular or interrupted mattress sutures, and conclude with a mandatory digital rectal examination.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Anal incontinence to flatus or liquid and solid faeces.
Rectovaginal fistula, perineal wound breakdown, and severe pelvic infection.
Severe chronic perineal pain, introital dyspareunia, and psychological fear of future vaginal birth.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Prescribe daily stool softeners (lactulose) and high-fibre diet for 10 to 14 days to prevent straining.
Administer broad-spectrum prophylactic antibiotics (cephalosporin and metronidazole) to minimise wound infection.
Advise local ice packs, warm sitz baths, and pelvic floor physiotherapy review at 6 to 12 weeks.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: A formal digital rectal examination is mandatory both before starting the repair to classify the injury and after completing skin closure to confirm lumen integrity.
If immediate repair is missed following delivery, repair should be delayed for 12 weeks to allow acute tissue edema, infection, and inflammation to subside.

viva.q: How is a third-degree perineal tear subclassified?
viva.a: Grade 3a involves less than 50% of the external anal sphincter thickness; 3b involves more than 50% of the external sphincter; 3c involves both external and internal anal sphincter disruption.

viva.q: What are the two accepted surgical techniques for repairing a torn external anal sphincter?
viva.a: The end-to-end approximation technique (for partial or full tears) and the overlapping technique (for complete full-thickness disruption of the muscle bellies).

viva.q: Why must an end-of-procedure digital rectal examination always be carried out?
viva.a: To confirm that the anal sphincter tone is reconstituted and to verify that no sutures have breached the rectal lumen, which would create a tract for rectovaginal fistula.

image.brief: Anatomical schematic of fourth-degree perineal tear repair showing layered closure of anorectal mucosa, internal anal sphincter mattress sutures, and overlapping external sphincter repair.

items.summary: Uterus-sparing surgical repair for uterovaginal prolapse and cervical elongation involving cervical amputation and anterior transposition of the cardinal ligaments.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Conservative gynaecological operation designed to treat uterine descent and supravaginal cervical elongation while preserving the uterine corpus.
Combines preliminary dilatation and curettage, amputation of the elongated cervix, plication of Mackenrodt ligaments anteriorly, and anterior colporrhaphy.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: First-degree or second-degree uterovaginal prolapse with prominent supravaginal cervical elongation in women wishing to conserve the uterus.
Symptomatic cystocele associated with marked cervical descent in patients not desiring hysterectomy.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Patient placed in dorsal lithotomy position under regional or general anaesthesia.
Surgical prep and drape of the perineum and vagina, with bladder emptied by catheterization.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Grasp anterior cervical lip with a vulsellum and sound the uterus to determine cavity and cervical lengths.
Perform preliminary dilatation and curettage (D&C) to exclude endometrial premalignancy and prevent cervical stenosis.
Make a triangular or inverted-T incision over the anterior vaginal wall and a transverse incision around the cervix at the cervicovaginal junction.
Dissect the bladder reflection superiorly off the anterior cervix up to the uterovesical fold of peritoneum.
Clamp, divide, and transfix the descending cervical branches and Mackenrodt (cardinal) ligaments bilaterally.
Amputate the elongated cervix at the level of the internal os using a sharp scalpel.
Suture the right Mackenrodt ligament stump across the anterior lower uterine segment, and overlap the left Mackenrodt stump securely over it.
Reconstruct a neocervix by inverting the anterior and posterior vaginal mucosal flaps over the cut cervical stump using Sturmdorf sutures.
Perform anterior colporrhaphy to plicate the pubocervical fascia and complete the procedure with colpoperineorrhaphy if required.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Intraoperative haemorrhage from the descending cervical branches of the uterine vessels.
Accidental bladder or rectal injury during deep fascial dissection.
Postoperative cervical stenosis, haematometra, and secondary dysmenorrhoea.
Obstetric complications in subsequent pregnancies: Cervical incompetence leading to mid-trimester loss, cervical dystocia necessitating caesarean birth.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Pack the vagina lightly with antiseptic gauze for 24 hours and maintain Foley catheter drainage.
Pass a sterile uterine sound at the 6-week outpatient follow-up to verify cervical canal patency and exclude stenosis.
Advise avoidance of heavy straining and intercourse for 6 weeks.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Shirodkar modification: Extends dissection to the pouch of Douglas, divides uterosacral ligaments, and anchors them anteriorly to repair accompanying enterocele.
Sturmdorf sutures are specialized inverting triradiate sutures that draw the vaginal epithelium cleanly over the raw amputated cervical lip to form a smooth neocervix.

viva.q: What are the essential operative components of the classic Manchester operation?
viva.a: Preliminary D&C, anterior colporrhaphy, bilateral clamping and division of Mackenrodt ligaments, amputation of the elongated cervix, anterior cross-plication of Mackenrodt ligaments, and Sturmdorf flap closure.

viva.q: What is the function of the Sturmdorf suture in Fothergill surgery?
viva.a: It is an inverting suture that draws the cut edges of the anterior and posterior vaginal mucosal walls into the endocervical canal, neatly epithelialising the raw amputated cervical stump to create a neocervix.

viva.q: Why is the Manchester operation rarely performed in women desiring future pregnancies?
viva.a: Cervical amputation significantly impairs cervical integrity, predisposing to mid-trimester miscarriage and preterm birth, or causes dense scarring leading to cervical dystocia during labour.

image.brief: Surgical steps diagram of Manchester operation showing cervical amputation, anterior cross-suturing of Mackenrodt ligaments over the lower uterine segment, and Sturmdorf inverting sutures.

items.summary: Retropubic mid-urethral polypropylene mesh sling placed without tension to treat genuine female stress urinary incontinence.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Minimally invasive retropubic sling procedure for female stress urinary incontinence (SUI).
Places a macroporous polypropylene mesh tape beneath the mid-urethra, which acts as a dynamic backboard supporting the urethra during physical coughing or straining.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Urodynamic stress urinary incontinence significantly impairing quality of life.
Stress incontinence associated with pelvic organ prolapse or persistent after failed conservative pelvic floor muscle training.
Recurrent stress urinary incontinence following prior failed anti-incontinence operations.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Patient in lithotomy position with hips moderately flexed under local, regional, or light general anaesthesia.
Administer intravenous prophylactic antibiotics and catheterise the bladder to drain urine completely.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Make two small transverse suprapubic incisions 1 to 1.5 cm long, sited 6 cm apart immediately above the superior pubic symphyseal border.
Infiltrate anterior vaginal mucosa and bilateral paraurethral spaces with local anaesthetic containing dilute adrenaline.
Make a 1.5 cm vertical sagittal incision over the anterior vaginal wall at the level of the mid-urethra.
Dissect paraurethral tunnels sharply and bluntly towards the inferior margin of the pubic ramus.
Insert a rigid metallic catheter guide into the Foley catheter to deflect the bladder neck contralaterally.
Introduce the curved TVT trocar through the paraurethral space, hugging the posterior aspect of the pubic bone through the space of Retzius to emerge at the suprapubic incision.
Perform mandatory cystoscopy with bladder distended by 200 to 250 mL saline to verify bladder and urethral integrity.
Pass the contralateral needle in identical fashion and repeat rigid cystoscopy.
Adjust the tape tension-free beneath the mid-urethra, leaving the thickness of a Metzenbaum scissor blade between tape and urethra.
Cut trocars flush with the abdominal skin, leaving the polypropylene mesh in situ, and close vaginal and abdominal incisions with absorbable sutures.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Intraoperative bladder or urethral puncture by the passing trocars.
Retropubic space haematoma or external iliac vascular injury.
Postoperative acute urinary retention or de novo urgency and urge incontinence.
Delayed vaginal mesh extrusion, urethral erosion, or suprapubic wound abscess.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Remove urinary catheter within 2 to 4 hours post-procedure and conduct a voiding trial.
Verify spontaneous voiding and ensure minimal residual urine before discharging the patient.
Instruct patient to avoid heavy lifting, vigorous exercise, and intercourse for 6 weeks.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Termed 'tension-free' because the synthetic mesh is not sutured or anchored to bone or fascia, relying on tissue ingrowth and gentle frictional hold.
Performing a cystourethroscopy after each trocar pass is an absolute medicolegal standard to identify and manage unsuspected bladder perforation.

viva.q: Why is rigid cystoscopy mandatory during a tension-free vaginal tape (TVT) procedure?
viva.a: Because the trocars traverse the blind retropubic space of Retzius; cystourethroscopy is required to rule out bladder or urethral perforation before the sling is adjusted.

viva.q: What should be done if a trocar is seen entering the bladder during intraoperative cystoscopy?
viva.a: Withdraw the needle immediately, re-introduce it along the correct retropubic pathway, repeat cystoscopy to verify integrity, and maintain catheter drainage until healed.

image.brief: Medical diagram of female pelvis showing the retropubic tension-free vaginal tape (TVT) forming a U-shaped sling beneath the mid-urethra and exiting through twin suprapubic punctures.

items.summary: Mid-urethral mesh sling passed through bilateral obturator foramina to treat stress urinary incontinence while avoiding the retropubic space.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Minimally invasive sling procedure that places a polypropylene mesh tape beneath the mid-urethra via the obturator foramina.
Provides hammock-like suburethral support with reduced risks of bladder, bowel, and major vascular injuries compared to retropubic TVT.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Objective female stress urinary incontinence unresponsive to conservative pelvic floor exercises.
Stress incontinence in patients with prior pelvic surgery or scarred retropubic space of Retzius.
Stress incontinence combined with pelvic organ prolapse repair.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Patient in dorsal lithotomy position with thighs hyperflexed (100 to 110 degrees) under regional or general anaesthesia.
Aseptic preparation of perineum, groin creases, and upper thighs, with Foley catheter drainage.

groups.label: Outside-in technique
bullets: Make small stab incisions in the bilateral genitofemoral groin creases at the level of the clitoris, lateral to the ischiopubic ramus.
Make a 1.5 cm sagittal incision over the mid-urethral anterior vaginal wall and dissect bilateral tunnels to the inferior pubic rami.
Introduce the helical Emmet-like needle through the groin stab incision, traversing obturator membrane and puborectalis towards an index finger in the vaginal incision.
Attach the tape to the needle tip and withdraw it outward to position the sling beneath the urethra.

groups.label: Inside-out technique
bullets: Pass the winged guide and helical passer from the suburethral vaginal dissection outward through the obturator membrane to exit at the groin stab incision.
Pull the tape through, adjust it tension-free beneath the mid-urethra, and trim redundant tape flush with the skin.
Close the anterior vaginal incision with absorbable sutures (Vicryl 2-0).

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Postoperative thigh, inner groin, or adductor muscle pain and transient obturator neuropraxia.
Vaginal sulcus mesh extrusion or erosion.
Transient urinary retention, de novo urinary urgency, or lower urinary tract infection.
Rare bladder or urethral puncture.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Perform a post-procedure voiding trial and verify minimal post-void residual urine volume before discharge.
Prescribe short-course analgesics and advise avoidance of strenuous physical activity and intercourse for 4 to 6 weeks.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Because the transobturator path avoids traversing the retropubic space of Retzius, risks of visceral bladder and pelvic vessel injuries are significantly lower than with TVT.
Hyperflexion of the hips at 100 to 110 degrees during positioning ensures safe passage of the helical trocars away from the obturator neurovascular canal.

viva.q: What is the key anatomical advantage of trans-obturator tape (TOT) over retropubic TVT?
viva.a: TOT passes through the obturator membranes rather than traversing the retro-pubic space of Retzius, significantly reducing the risk of bladder perforation, bowel injury, and major pelvic vessel hemorrhage.

viva.q: What specific postoperative complication is more common with TOT compared to TVT?
viva.a: Transient inner thigh, groin, and adductor muscle pain, secondary to needle passage through the obturator membrane and gracilis/adductor brevis muscle insertions.

image.brief: Cross-sectional pelvic diagram of trans-obturator tape showing mesh traversing the obturator foramina bilaterally to form a horizontal hammock beneath the mid-urethra.

items.summary: Core surgical principles of safe peritoneal entry, creation of carbon dioxide pneumoperitoneum, and primary and secondary port placements in gynaecology.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Minimally invasive endoscopic access into the peritoneal cavity to inspect and operate on pelvic reproductive organs.
Involves safe entry using closed (Veress needle) or open (Hasson) techniques, CO2 insufflation, and ergonomic port layout.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Diagnostic evaluation: Unexplained infertility, chronic pelvic pain, suspected endometriosis, and ectopic pregnancy.
Therapeutic interventions: Salpingectomy, cystectomy, myomectomy, adhesiolysis, and laparoscopic hysterectomy.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Patient in modified lithotomy position under general endotracheal anaesthesia with empty bladder and stomach.
Table kept horizontal during initial entry, then adjusted to steep Trendelenburg position (20 to 30 degrees) once ports are secured.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Make a vertical or smile incision at the base of the umbilicus, which represents the thinnest zone of the abdominal wall.
Insert a tested Veress needle at 45 degrees in non-obese or 90 degrees in obese patients, noting two distinct clicks as it penetrates rectus sheath and peritoneum.
Perform safety checks: Double click test, aspiration test (no blood or bowel contents), and saline hanging drop test.
Connect CO2 insufflation tubing and confirm opening pressure is low (less than 10 mm Hg).
Insufflate carbon dioxide to a pressure of 20 to 25 mm Hg to create a tense abdominal cushion for primary trocar insertion.
Introduce primary 10 mm optical trocar, reduce pressure to 12 to 15 mm Hg, and insert laparoscope.
Perform 360-degree peritoneal inspection immediately beneath the entry site to rule out vascular or visceral trocar injury.
Place secondary ancillary ports (5 mm to 7 mm) in the lower quadrants under direct laparoscopic vision, transilluminating the abdominal wall to avoid inferior epigastric vessels.
Perform the planned operative procedure, then withdraw secondary ports under direct vision to confirm hemostasis.
Evacuate pneumoperitoneum completely, close the fascial sheath for ports 10 mm or larger with absorbable sutures, and appose skin.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Major vascular injury to the abdominal aorta, inferior vena cava, or common iliac vessels during trocar insertion.
Iatrogenic bowel or bladder perforation from Veress needle or sharp trocars.
Subcutaneous emphysema, gas embolism, or hypercarbia from CO2 insufflation.
Incisional hernia at unclosed 10 mm or larger port sites.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Monitor vital signs, oxygen saturation, and shoulder tip pain (referred phrenic pain from diaphragmatic CO2 irritation).
Encourage early oral fluids and mobilization, discharging uncomplicated day-care cases within 24 hours.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Palmer point: Alternative entry site located 3 cm below the left costal margin in the midclavicular line, indicated in suspected periumbilical adhesions or hepatosplenomegaly.
Hasson open technique: Direct cutdown under vision through the umbilical fascia and peritoneum, highly recommended in patients with previous laparotomy scars.

viva.q: What safety tests confirm the correct intraperitoneal placement of a Veress needle?
viva.a: Feeling two distinct tactile clicks, syringe aspiration showing no blood or enteric fluid, the hanging drop test where saline is drawn into the cavity, and an initial gas insufflation pressure below 10 mm Hg.

viva.q: Where is Palmer's point located, and when is it indicated for laparoscopic access?
viva.a: Located 3 cm below the left subcostal margin in the midclavicular line; used for primary peritoneal entry when umbilical adhesions are suspected due to previous midline scars or multiple laparotomies.

viva.q: Why must secondary laparoscopic trocars be inserted under direct visual control?
viva.a: To avoid accidental puncture of the inferior epigastric arteries running along the lateral rectus sheath and to prevent direct mechanical perforation of pelvic viscera.

image.brief: Diagram illustrating laparoscopic entry at the umbilicus, showing Veress needle insertion angle, layers of anterior abdominal wall, and secondary port placements avoiding inferior epigastric vessels.

items.summary: Complete laparoscopic surgical excision of the uterus and cervix with intraperitoneal vault closure using advanced electrothermal energy devices.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Minimally invasive surgical procedure where the entire hysterectomy, including separation of all pedicles, colpotomy, and vaginal vault closure, is completed laparoscopically.
Performed using specialized laparoscopic bipolar, ultrasonic, or advanced vessel-sealing instruments with vaginal specimen retrieval.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Symptomatic uterine leiomyomas, adenomyosis, or abnormal uterine bleeding refractory to medical management.
Premalignant and early malignant diseases: Atypical endometrial hyperplasia, early stage I endometrial cancer.
Chronic pelvic pain secondary to severe endometriosis in women completing childbearing.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Steep Trendelenburg lithotomy position under general endotracheal anaesthesia with indwelling urinary catheter.
Insert a rigid uterine manipulator with a delineating cervical cup (e.g. Clermont-Ferrand, Rumi, or Hohl manipulator) to mobilize the uterus and delineate the fornices.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Establish pneumoperitoneum and place umbilical optical port and three lower quadrant ancillary 5 mm ports.
Manipulate the uterus cranially and laterally to stretch the contralateral adnexal pedicle.
Coagulate and divide the round ligament with advanced bipolar energy and incise the anterior broad ligament leaf.
Coagulate and divide the utero-ovarian ligament and fallopian tube near the cornu (or infundibulopelvic ligament if performing BSO).
Dissect and push down the uterovesical peritoneal fold, gently reflecting the urinary bladder below the cervical cup rim.
Skeletonise the uterine vascular bundle at the level of the internal os, verifying ureteric location and peristalsis.
Coagulate and divide the uterine vessels flush against the cervical margin.
Coagulate and transect the cardinal (Mackenrodt) and uterosacral ligaments bilaterally.
Perform circumferential colpotomy along the manipulator cup rim using monopolar hook or harmonic energy to detach the cervix.
Extract the uterus vaginally through the open introitus, or via contained in-bag morcellation if too large.
Close the vaginal vault laparoscopically or transvaginally with barbed or braided absorbable sutures (Vicryl 1), and verify hemostasis.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Thermal or transection injury to the lower pelvic ureter during uterine artery and cardinal ligament coagulation.
Bladder laceration during anterior dissection, or bowel perforation from electrosurgical instruments.
Vaginal vault haematoma, cuff dehiscence, or secondary pelvic infection.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Remove urinary catheter within 12 to 24 hours and maintain multimodal analgesia.
Encourage early ambulation and oral diet resumption, discharging patient within 24 to 48 hours.
Counsel avoidance of vaginal intercourse and strenuous exercise for 6 to 8 weeks.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Active identification of ureteral peristalsis at the pelvic brim and lateral to the uterine vessels prevents silent thermal ureteric injury.
A properly positioned uterine manipulator cup provides cranial elevation that increases the safe working distance between the cervix and ureter.

viva.q: What defines a total laparoscopic hysterectomy (TLH) compared to LAVH?
viva.a: In TLH, the entire procedure, including uterine vessel coagulation, cardinal ligament transection, circumferential colpotomy, and vaginal vault closure, is completed laparoscopically.

viva.q: How does a uterine manipulator with a cervical cup protect adjacent organs during TLH?
viva.a: It provides cephalad elevation and lateral deflection of the uterus, stretching pedicles and pushing the ureters laterally away from energy application zones, while marking the safe colpotomy margin.

image.brief: Laparoscopic intraoperative view of TLH showing bipolar coagulation of the skeletonised uterine artery, with uterine manipulator cup delineating the cervicovaginal junction.

items.summary: Hybrid surgical hysterectomy where upper uterine and adnexal pedicles are secured laparoscopically, while lower pedicles, colpotomy, and removal are completed vaginally.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Combined minimally invasive operation where the upper uterine ligaments and adnexa are mobilised laparoscopically, and the remainder is completed transvaginally.
Enables transvaginal hysterectomy in patients with limited vaginal access, pelvic adhesions, or concurrent adnexal pathology.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Benign uterine conditions (AUB, fibroids, adenomyosis) with minimal pelvic floor descent.
Anticipated upper pelvic adhesions from previous pelvic surgery or endometriosis unmanageable purely through vaginal surgery.
Need for concurrent bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy in patients undergoing vaginal hysterectomy.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Trendelenburg lithotomy position under general endotracheal anaesthesia with sterile preparation of abdomen and perineum.
Insert Foley catheter and fit a uterine manipulator to facilitate laparoscopic pelvic exposure.

groups.label: Laparoscopic stage
bullets: Insert laparoscope and secondary lower quadrant ports under pneumoperitoneum.
Coagulate and divide round ligaments bilaterally with bipolar or advanced energy devices.
Open the broad ligament leaves and dissect the uterovesical fold of peritoneum, pushing the bladder downward.
Secure and divide the infundibulopelvic ligaments (or utero-ovarian pedicles if ovaries are conserved).
Skeletonise the ascending branches of the uterine vessels.

groups.label: Vaginal stage
bullets: Move to perineal approach, apply vulsellum traction to cervix, and incise cervicovaginal junction circumferentially.
Enter the previously dissected anterior uterovesical pouch and sharp entry into posterior pouch of Douglas.
Clamp, divide, and transfix the Mackenrodt (cardinal) and uterosacral ligaments bilaterally with Vicryl No. 1.
Ligate and divide the remaining uterine vessels from below.
Deliver the uterus and adnexa vaginally, inspect pedicles, and close the vaginal vault transvaginally with absorbable sutures.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Iatrogenic thermal or mechanical injury to ureters, bladder, or rectosigmoid bowel.
Intraoperative haemorrhage or uncontrolled broad ligament vessel bleeding.
Pelvic haematoma, vault cellulitis, or delayed vault prolapse.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Remove Foley catheter after 12 to 24 hours and maintain adequate analgesia.
Encourage early ambulation and counsel avoidance of strenuous physical activity and intercourse for 6 weeks.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: LAVH bridges laparoscopic and vaginal surgery, allowing the surgeon to inspect the upper abdomen, lyse adnexal adhesions, and divide cornual pedicles before transitioning to the familiar vaginal route.
Uterine vessel ligation can be performed either laparoscopically or vaginally depending on surgical comfort and anatomical descent.

viva.q: What are the primary clinical indications for choosing LAVH over standard vaginal hysterectomy?
viva.a: Suspected pelvic adhesions from previous surgeries or endometriosis, nulliparity or lack of uterine descent, and the necessity to perform concurrent bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.

viva.q: At what anatomical step does the laparoscopic phase transition to the vaginal phase in LAVH?
viva.a: After dividing the round ligaments, adnexal or infundibulopelvic ligaments, and mobilising the bladder reflection, the surgeon shifts to the perineal field to perform colpotomy and secure the cardinal ligaments.

image.brief: Diagram showing the hybrid technique of LAVH, illustrating laparoscopic division of upper round and adnexal pedicles combined with vaginal clamping of cardinal ligaments.

items.summary: Transcervical endoscopic visualization of the endocervical canal and uterine cavity for diagnostic inspection and therapeutic intra-cavity interventions.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Endoscopic examination of the uterine cavity using an illuminated optical hysteroscope passed through the cervix under continuous distension.
Employed as the diagnostic gold standard for intrauterine pathology and as a minimally invasive surgical route for endometrial and intracavitary procedures.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) in women over 40 years, or under 40 years refractory to medical treatment.
Postmenopausal bleeding with endometrial thickness 4 mm or greater on transvaginal ultrasonography.
Postcoital bleeding, recurrent miscarriage, or secondary infertility evaluation.

Therapeutic procedures: Endometrial polyp resection, submucous myomectomy, adhesiolysis for Asherman syndrome, septoplasty for septate uterus, and retrieval of lost intrauterine contraceptive devices.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Patient in dorsal lithotomy position under local paracervical block, conscious sedation, or general anaesthesia.
Can be performed as an outpatient day-care procedure using miniature (less than 5 mm) continuous-flow instruments.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Perform bimanual examination to ascertain uterine size, axis, and anteversion or retroversion.
Expose the cervix with a speculum or employ the 'no-touch' vaginoscopic approach without speculum or tenaculum.
Introduce the hysteroscope into the external cervical os under direct visual guidance.
Infuse distension media (normal saline for bipolar electrosurgery, or CO2 for diagnostic inspection) to maintain clear panoramic visualization.
Inspect the endocervical canal, internal os, uterine cavity, posterior wall, anterior wall, bilateral lateral walls, and tubal ostia systematically.
Introduce operating micro-instruments (graspers, scissors, or bipolar resectoscope electrode) through the working channel.
Perform required therapeutic interventions: Biopsy, polypectomy, myomectomy, adhesiolysis, or foreign body retrieval.
Withdraw the instrument under vision, document findings, and assess for post-procedural vaginal bleeding.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Iatrogenic uterine wall perforation, with risk of thermal or mechanical bladder or bowel injury.
Cervical laceration and excessive intraoperative haemorrhage.
Fluid overload syndrome, dilutional hyponatraemia, cerebral oedema, or air/gas embolism.
Postoperative endometritis, pelvic infection, and secondary intrauterine synechiae.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Monitor patient in day-care recovery for 2 to 4 hours assessing vital signs and lochial spotting.
Prescribe simple oral analgesics and counsel that mild menstrual-like cramping and pink spotting may persist for a few days.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Normal saline is the distension medium of choice for operative hysteroscopy; it is isotonic, compatible with bipolar electrosurgery, and reduces hyponatraemia risk.
Non-electrolyte media like 1.5% glycine or 5% mannitol carry significant risks of systemic fluid absorption, acute hyponatremic encephalopathy, and pulmonary oedema.

viva.q: What is the 'no-touch' or vaginoscopic technique in hysteroscopy?
viva.a: A modern outpatient method where the hysteroscope is introduced directly into the vaginal introitus and guided into the cervical canal using fluid distension, avoiding the use of a vaginal speculum, tenaculum, or cervical dilatation.

viva.q: Why is normal saline preferred over 1.5% glycine as a distension medium in modern operative hysteroscopy?
viva.a: Normal saline is an isotonic electrolyte solution that permits safe use of bipolar electrosurgery and avoids the life-threatening hyponatraemia, cerebral oedema, and fluid overload risks associated with glycine absorption.

viva.q: What is the cut-off for endometrial thickness prompting hysteroscopic evaluation in postmenopausal bleeding?
viva.a: An endometrial thickness of 4 mm or greater on transvaginal ultrasonography in a postmenopausal woman warrants hysteroscopic evaluation and targeted endometrial biopsy to rule out endometrial carcinoma.

image.brief: Medical diagram of an operative hysteroscope showing continuous inflow and outflow fluid sheath channels, working channel with electrosurgical loop, optical light cable, and panoramic endocavity view.

items.summary: Transcervical female permanent sterilisation involving hysteroscopic placement of nickel-titanium micro-inserts into the proximal tubal ostia to induce fibrotic occlusion.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Permanent non-incisional female sterilisation method performed under hysteroscopic vision without abdominal surgery.
Deploys micro-inserts into the interstitial-isthmic segments of both fallopian tubes to induce chronic foreign-body tissue ingrowth and complete luminal occlusion.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Permanent female contraception in women requesting irreversible sterilisation.
Particularly suited for women with severe medical contraindications to general anaesthesia or extensive abdominal adhesions precluding laparoscopic tubal ligation.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Patient in dorsal lithotomy position under local paracervical block or light sedation in an outpatient procedure room.
Perform during the early proliferative phase of the menstrual cycle when the endometrium is thinnest to optimize tubal ostial visualisation.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Introduce a diagnostic hysteroscope into the uterine cavity under normal saline distension and identify both tubal ostia.
Pass the flexible delivery catheter carrying the micro-insert through the working channel into the tubal ostium.
Advance the micro-insert until the demarcation indicator reaches the ostial plane, anchoring into the proximal fallopian tube.
Release the outer expanding nickel-titanium (nitinol) coil and inner stainless steel core containing polyethylene terephthalate (PET) fibres.
Confirm proper placement with 3 to 8 outer coil trailing loops visible in the uterine cavity.
Repeat the identical deployment in the contralateral tubal ostium.
Withdraw the hysteroscope and advise the patient to maintain alternative contraception for 3 months.
Perform a confirmatory hysterosalpingogram (HSG) or pelvic radiograph at 3 months to document bilateral tubal occlusion and proper coil position.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Improper placement, coil migration into the peritoneal cavity, or failure of tubal cannulation.
Severe chronic pelvic pain, cramping, and heavy irregular uterine bleeding.
Systemic allergic reaction to nickel components of the nitinol alloy.
Iatrogenic uterine or tubal wall perforation, pelvic sepsis, or unintended intrauterine and ectopic pregnancy.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Discharge patient after 1 to 2 hours of post-procedure observation with simple analgesics.
Maintain reliable alternative barrier or hormonal contraception for a full 3 months post-procedure.
Conduct confirmatory hysterosalpingography at 3 months before permitting cessation of alternative contraception.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Luminal tubal occlusion is not immediate; it requires approximately 3 months for local fibroblast ingrowth stimulated by the PET fibres to form an impermeable scar.
Due to long-term post-market safety concerns regarding chronic pelvic pain, nickel hypersensitivity, and device migration, Essure was discontinued commercially.

viva.q: What is the biological mechanism of tubal occlusion induced by the Essure device?
viva.a: Polyethylene terephthalate fibres inside the stainless steel coil stimulate a foreign body reaction, promoting dense fibrotic tissue ingrowth over 3 months that completely occludes the tubal lumen.

viva.q: Why is alternative contraception mandatory for 3 months following Essure insertion?
viva.a: Because permanent fibrotic closure takes up to 12 weeks to complete; alternative contraception must be used until bilateral tubal occlusion is confirmed by hysterosalpingography at 3 months.

image.brief: Hysteroscopic view showing the ostium of the fallopian tube with an expanded metallic Essure micro-insert showing trailing nitinol coils anchored in the proximal intramural tube.

items.summary: Destruction of the endometrial basalis layer using thermal, radiofrequency, or cryoablative energy to treat heavy menstrual bleeding in benign disease.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Minimally invasive destruction of the full endometrial lining and underlying superficial myometrium to induce amenorrhoea or hypomenorrhoea in abnormal uterine bleeding.
Categorised into hysteroscopic first-generation methods requiring skilled resectoscopic guidance and automated second-generation non-hysteroscopic global ablation devices.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia) due to benign causes refractory to medical therapies in women wishing to avoid major hysterectomy.
Patient has completed childbearing and has normal endometrial biopsy ruling out hyperplasia and malignancy.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Perform procedure in early proliferative phase or pre-treat with GnRH agonists for 4 to 8 weeks to thin the endometrium to under 4 mm.
Patient in dorsal lithotomy position under local paracervical block, conscious sedation, or general anaesthesia.

groups.label: First-generation hysteroscopic methods
bullets: Transcervical resection of the endometrium (TCRE): Introduce resectoscope under glycine distension and resect endometrium down to 4 to 5 mm using a diathermic wire loop or rollerball electrode.
Nd:YAG laser photocoagulation: Deliver laser energy under continuous hysteroscopic irrigation to vaporise and coagulate endometrium.

groups.label: Second-generation global ablation methods
bullets: Microwave endometrial ablation (MEA): Deliver 9.2 GHz microwaves heating tissue to 92 degrees Celsius for 1 to 4 minutes to achieve 6 mm coagulation depth.
Thermal balloon endometrial ablation (TBEA): Insert a silicone balloon filled with 5% dextrose, heat to 87 degrees Celsius at 160 mm Hg pressure for 8 minutes to ablate 4 to 5 mm depth.
Cryoablation: Apply cryoprobe cooled to minus 90 degrees Celsius for 10 minutes to freeze the endometrium to a depth of 10 mm.
Hydrothermal ablation: Circulate free-flowing heated saline at low intrauterine pressure under hysteroscopic visualization.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: First-generation risks: Fluid overload, dilutional hyponatraemia, cerebral oedema, and uterine wall perforation.
Second-generation risks: Acute uterine cramping, post-procedure nausea, pelvic infection, and accidental genital thermal burns.
Late risks: Haematometra secondary to cervical stenosis, post-ablation tubal sterilization syndrome, and delayed endometrial cancer diagnosis.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Prescribe oral analgesics and inform the patient that serosanguinous vaginal discharge will occur for 2 to 4 weeks.
Emphasise that endometrial ablation is not a contraceptive method; reliable permanent or barrier contraception remains mandatory.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Contraindications include active pelvic infection, desire for future childbearing, endometrial hyperplasia or malignancy, and distorted uterine cavity exceeding device limits.
Pregnancy following endometrial ablation carries high risks of placenta accreta spectrum, ectopic pregnancy, uterine rupture, and perinatal loss.

viva.q: What are the major advantages of second-generation over first-generation endometrial ablation devices?
viva.a: Second-generation devices do not require skilled hysteroscopic resectoscopic training, eliminate the risk of hyponatremic fluid overload from distension media, are faster, and can be performed in outpatient settings.

viva.q: Why must women use reliable contraception after undergoing endometrial ablation?
viva.a: Because ovulation continues; any subsequent pregnancy is hazardous, carrying severe risks of morbidly adherent placenta accreta, ectopic pregnancy, preterm labour, and uterine rupture.

image.brief: Medical illustration comparing endometrial ablation modalities showing thermal balloon system inside the uterine cavity and rollerball resectoscope electrode ablating the endometrium.

items.summary: Outpatient thermal ablation of benign cervical ectropion and erosion using rapidly expanding cryogenic nitrous oxide gas.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Non-invasive outpatient cryosurgical procedure that freezes cervical surface epithelium to treat chronic benign cervical ectropion.
Employs compressed liquid nitrous oxide gas delivered through a metallic cryoprobe to cause intracellular ice crystallization and cell death.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Symptomatic cervical ectropion (cervical erosion) causing persistent excessive vaginal discharge or postcoital spotting.
Chronic non-specific cervicitis unresponsive to repeated medical antimicrobial therapy, with prior negative cervical cytology.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Conducted as an outpatient procedure in dorsal lithotomy position without requiring local or general anaesthesia.
Expose the cervix with a large bivalve Cusco or Sims speculum and cleanse the surface with saline.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Select a cryoprobe tip with contours that adequately cover the entire cervical ectropion lesion.
Apply water-soluble lubricant to the probe tip to ensure efficient thermal contact with the cervical epithelium.
Position probe firmly against the cervix and activate refrigerant flow of liquid nitrous oxide.
Observe development of an ice ball extending 4 to 5 mm beyond the margins of the probe.
Freeze at minus 45 degrees Celsius for 120 seconds, allow passive complete thawing, and repeat freezing at minus 45 degrees Celsius for another 120 seconds.
Allow complete thawing before gently detaching the cryoprobe from the cervix to prevent tearing mucosal tissue.
Inspect the cervix to ensure hemostasis and discharge the patient home immediately.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Mild intraoperative vasovagal reaction or pelvic uterine cramping.
Copious watery vaginal discharge persisting for 2 to 3 weeks during tissue sloughing.
Secondary cervical infection, spotting, or rare cervical stenosis.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Reassure the patient regarding expected profuse watery vaginal discharge for 2 to 3 weeks.
Instruct the patient to avoid vaginal tampons, douching, and sexual intercourse for 3 to 4 weeks until complete re-epithelialisation.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Mechanism: Rapid freezing to minus 45 degrees Celsius causes cellular dehydration, ice crystal formation, and irreversible membrane lysis.
Never perform cryocautery without prior normal cervical cytology and colposcopy to rule out cervical intraepithelial neoplasia and invasive carcinoma.

viva.q: What is the physical mechanism of cell death during cervical cryocautery?
viva.a: Rapid freezing produces intracellular water crystallization, hyperosmolar cellular dehydration, protein denaturation, and thermal shock leading to coagulative tissue necrosis.

viva.q: What typical postoperative symptom should the patient be counselled about following cervical cryocautery?
viva.a: Profuse, watery, serous vaginal discharge lasting for 2 to 3 weeks as the necrotic frozen cervical epithelial slough separates and regenerating squamous epithelium covers the cervix.

image.brief: Clinical setup of cervical cryocautery showing handheld cryogun connected to nitrous oxide gas cylinder, with silver probe tip resting against the uterine cervix.

title.en: Large Loop Excision of Transformation Zone (LLETZ)

items.summary: Outpatient electrosurgical loop excision of the cervical transformation zone for the histological diagnosis and treatment of high-grade cervical dysplasia.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Outpatient excisional procedure utilising a thin wire loop powered by electrosurgical diathermy to resect the cervical transformation zone.
Provides both therapeutic clearance of dysplastic cervical epithelium and an intact histological specimen to evaluate surgical margins.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN 2 or CIN 3) identified on colposcopically directed biopsies.
Persistent CIN 1 lasting more than 2 years in adult women.
Discrepancy between cervical smear cytology and colposcopic biopsy findings, or unsatisfactory colposcopy with suspected high-grade lesions.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Patient in dorsal lithotomy position with return grounding pad attached to the thigh.
Insert non-conductive insulated Cusco speculum fitted with a smoke evacuator tube.
Infiltrate cervical stroma with local anaesthetic containing a vasoconstrictor (2% lignocaine with 1:200,000 adrenaline).

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Apply 5% acetic acid and Lugol's iodine solution to clearly demarcate the outer borders of the abnormal transformation zone.
Select an appropriately sized stainless steel or tungsten wire loop that spans the entire lesion.
Activate the cutting diathermy generator and pass the loop steadily through the cervix in a single continuous sweep to a depth under 10 mm.
Retrieve the intact disc of excised cervical tissue and place it on a labeled card orienting the 12 o'clock position for pathology.
Perform endocervical curettage if indicated to assess the superior canal margin.
Switch generator to coagulation mode and apply a 3 mm to 5 mm ball electrode over the crater bed to achieve meticulous hemostasis.
Apply Monsel ferric subsulphate paste to the excisional crater to provide additional chemical hemostasis.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Intraoperative or secondary postoperative haemorrhage occurring between days 7 and 10 upon eschar separation.
Infection manifesting as foul-smelling discharge or pelvic pain.
Cervical stenosis leading to dysmenorrhoea, haematometra, or difficulty with future cervical screening.
Obstetric risks in subsequent gestations: Small increased risk of mid-trimester miscarriage and preterm birth when excision depth exceeds 10 mm.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Instruct the patient to avoid vaginal tampons, heavy physical lifting, and sexual intercourse for 4 weeks.
Schedule repeat cytology and high-risk HPV co-testing 'test of cure' at 6 months post-procedure.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Excision should generally be restricted to less than 10 mm depth to preserve cervical structural integrity and prevent preterm birth.

Cervical conisation (cold-knife or laser cone) is preferred over LLETZ when microinvasive carcinoma is suspected, adenocarcinoma in situ is present, or the endocervical canal margin cannot be visualized.

viva.q: What is the primary advantage of LLETZ compared to ablative methods like cryocautery?
viva.a: LLETZ yields an intact histological tissue specimen that allows pathological assessment of lesion depth, exclusion of unsuspected invasive carcinoma, and evaluation of surgical margins.

viva.q: What is the significance of excision depth exceeding 10 mm during LLETZ?
viva.a: Excision depths exceeding 10 mm remove significant cervical stromal collagen, increasing the risk of cervical incompetence, mid-trimester miscarriage, and preterm pre-labour rupture of membranes in future pregnancies.

image.brief: Illustration of LLETZ procedure showing thin wire loop electrode excising the circular cervical transformation zone around the external os under colposcopic guidance.

items.summary: Outpatient blind aspiration sampling of the endometrium using a flexible polypropylene suction curette to evaluate abnormal uterine bleeding.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Minimally invasive office procedure for obtaining representative histological samples from the endometrial lining without requiring anaesthesia or cervical dilatation.
Widely utilised as the first-line investigation for abnormal uterine bleeding and postmenopausal bleeding.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) in women aged 40 years or older.
Postmenopausal bleeding with transvaginal ultrasound showing endometrial thickness 4 mm or greater.
Monitoring women on tamoxifen therapy or with high hereditary risk of endometrial malignancy (Lynch syndrome).

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Conducted as a quick outpatient procedure with the patient in dorsal lithotomy position.
Cleanse cervix with antiseptic solution; anaesthesia is usually unnecessary, though oral NSAIDs can be given beforehand.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Insert a bivalve Cusco speculum to visualise the external cervical os clearly.
Cleanse the ectocervix with sterile saline or antiseptic solution.
Introduce a sterile uterine sound gently if needed to confirm uterocervical axial length.
Advance the flexible Pipelle sheath through the external and internal os until resistance is felt at the uterine fundus.
Withdraw the internal piston fully backwards to create negative suction vacuum within the lumen.
Rotate the Pipelle 360 degrees while gently moving it back and forth between fundus and internal os to draw endometrial strips through the distal aperture.
Withdraw the device, push the internal plunger forward, and express collected endometrial tissue directly into a labeled container of 10% formalin for histology.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Transient uterine cramping pain and mild vasovagal lightheadedness during aspiration.
Inadequate or scanty tissue sample, particularly in atrophic postmenopausal endometrium, requiring formal hysteroscopy.
Very rare uterine perforation or post-procedural endometritis.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Allow patient to rest supine for 5 to 10 minutes before mobilising.
Reassure that slight spotting and mild cramps may persist for 24 hours.
Review histological findings to guide medical or surgical therapy.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Diagnostic accuracy exceeds 95% for detecting global endometrial carcinoma in postmenopausal women.
Blind Pipelle sampling may miss focal intrauterine pathologies (such as endometrial polyps or small submucous fibroids), which require diagnostic hysteroscopy.

viva.q: How does the Pipelle curette create suction to draw endometrial tissue?
viva.a: Once the cannula tip is positioned at the fundus, withdrawing the internal piston backwards creates a negative suction vacuum that draws endometrial tissue through the distal lateral port.

viva.q: What is the primary limitation of blind Pipelle endometrial sampling?
viva.a: It samples only a fraction of the total endometrial surface area; while highly sensitive for diffuse carcinoma, it can miss focal lesions such as small polyps or focal atypia.

items.summary: Targeted excision of small focal cervical epithelial and stromal tissue specimens using punch biopsy forceps to diagnose premalignant and malignant lesions.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Outpatient minor diagnostic procedure to obtain targeted tissue bites from suspicious cervical epithelial areas.
Employed under direct colposcopic vision to sample the most abnormal areas of the transformation zone for histopathology.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Clinically suspicious or ulcerated exophytic cervix on routine speculum inspection.
Cervical cytology reporting high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (CIN 2 or CIN 3) or adenocarcinoma in situ.
Abnormal colposcopic findings: Dense acetowhite epithelium, coarse punctation, coarse mosaicism, or atypical vessels.
Persistent chronic inflammatory cervical lesions unresponsive to repeated antibiotic courses.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Patient in dorsal lithotomy position under good direct lighting or colposcopic guidance.
Anaesthesia is usually not required as the ectocervix has minimal somatic pain innervation; mild sedation may be given if anxious.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Perform preliminary bimanual pelvic examination to assess uterine and pelvic status.
Insert a bivalve speculum to expose the cervix completely.
Apply 5% acetic acid and Lugol's iodine solution to highlight the most dysplastic areas.
Stabilise the anterior cervical lip gently with a tenaculum or vulsellum if the cervix is excessively mobile.
Position the sharp open jaws of the cervical punch biopsy forceps (e.g. Tischler or Kevorkian forceps) across the margin of the abnormal area.
Close the forceps jaws firmly to punch out a 2 to 3 mm bite of epithelium and underlying stroma cleanly.
Place the biopsy specimen immediately into a labeled specimen vial containing 10% neutral buffered formalin.
Achieve local hemostasis at the biopsy site by firm cotton swab pressure, silver nitrate application, or Monsel paste.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Local post-biopsy bleeding or persistent oozing from vascular stromal beds.
Mild lower abdominal pelvic cramping.
Secondary local cervical infection or discharge.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Instruct patient to avoid heavy lifting, vigorous exercise, tampons, and sexual intercourse for 48 to 72 hours.
Provide simple analgesics and advise the patient to return for histopathology results to plan definitive management.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Biopsies must be taken from the most severe colposcopic lesion, typically at the squamocolumnar junction near 12 or 6 o'clock.
Ensure each specimen includes sufficient underlying cervical stroma to allow the pathologist to evaluate for stromal invasion.

viva.q: Which areas of the abnormal cervix should be targeted during colposcopically directed punch biopsy?
viva.a: Target the areas showing the most abnormal colposcopic features, such as dense opaque acetowhite change, coarse punctation, coarse mosaicism, or atypical branching vessels, including the squamocolumnar margin.

viva.q: Why is the inclusion of underlying stroma critical in a cervical punch biopsy specimen?
viva.a: Adequate underlying stroma is essential for the pathologist to distinguish high-grade intraepithelial dysplasia (CIN 3) from early invasive microinvasive squamous cell carcinoma.

items.summary: Stepwise diagnostic curettage separating endocervical canal sampling from endometrial cavity curettage to evaluate and stage uterine bleeding and malignancy.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Diagnostic surgical procedure where endocervical curettings and endometrial curettings are harvested separately in sequential stages.
Designed to distinguish whether a neoplasm arises from or involves the endocervix versus the endometrial corpus.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Evaluation of postmenopausal bleeding to rule out endometrial carcinoma and determine whether cervical stromal invasion is present.
Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) refractory to medical treatment with suspected endometrial hyperplasia.
Staging workup in confirmed endometrial adenocarcinoma to evaluate for cervical extension (distinguishing Stage I from Stage II).

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Patient in dorsal lithotomy position under intravenous sedation, paracervical block, or light general anaesthesia.
Aseptic preparation and draping of perineum and vagina, with bladder emptied.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Expose the cervix with a posterior speculum and grasp the anterior lip with a tenaculum.
Step 1: Curette the endocervical canal first using a small Kevorkian or sharp curette before introducing any sound or dilator beyond the internal os.
Collect endocervical curettings and transfer immediately into Specimen Bottle 1 labeled 'Endocervical curettings'.
Step 2: Introduce a calibrated uterine sound through the internal os to determine uterine axis and cavity length.
Step 3: Sequentially dilate the internal cervical os with graduated Hegar dilators to allow curette entry.
Step 4: Systematically curette the uterine cavity (fundus, anterior wall, posterior wall, and lateral walls) using a sharp uterine curette.
Collect all endometrial tissue fragments and transfer into Specimen Bottle 2 labeled 'Endometrial curettings'.
Ensure hemostasis, remove instruments, and inspect for trauma.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Iatrogenic uterine wall perforation, with risk of visceral bladder or bowel injury.
Cervical laceration and excessive intraoperative bleeding.
Postoperative endometritis, pelvic infection, or secondary intrauterine synechiae (Asherman syndrome).

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Observe patient in day-care recovery for 2 to 4 hours assessing vital signs and vaginal lochial flow.
Advise the patient that light cramping and spotting may persist for a few days, and instruct avoidance of intercourse for 2 weeks.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: The critical technical rule is that endocervical curettage MUST precede uterine sounding and cervical dilatation to avoid contaminating the endocervical sample with dislodged endometrial tissue.
Largely superseded in modern outpatient gynaecology by Pipelle biopsy and diagnostic hysteroscopy with targeted biopsy.

viva.q: Why must the endocervical canal be curetted before the uterine sound is inserted in fractional curettage?
viva.a: To avoid mechanically pushing endometrial cells into the endocervical canal, which would produce a false-positive cervical involvement finding and erroneously upstage endometrial carcinoma from Stage I to Stage II.

viva.q: How does fractional curettage differentiate Stage I from Stage II endometrial carcinoma?
viva.a: Stage I is confined to the uterine corpus; if histological analysis of the separate endocervical fractional curettings reveals malignant glandular invasion into cervical stroma, the tumor is classified as Stage II.

title.en: Marsupialisation of Bartholin Cyst or Abscess

items.summary: Surgical incision and eversion of a symptomatic Bartholin duct cyst or abscess to form a permanent secretory drainage pouch while preserving the gland.

blocks.title: What it is
bullets: Definitive surgical procedure to treat a symptomatic retention cyst or acute abscess of the Bartholin gland duct.
Involves wide incision of the cyst and eversion of its epithelial edges to the vestibular mucosa, creating a permanent new ostium that preserves gland secretion.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Symptomatic or recurrent Bartholin gland duct cyst causing introital obstruction, discomfort during walking, or dyspareunia.
Acute Bartholin gland abscess presenting with severe throbbing vulval pain, erythema, and fluctuance.

blocks.title: Preparation and position
bullets: Patient in dorsal lithotomy position under local infiltration anaesthesia (1% lignocaine with or without adrenaline) or regional/sedation anaesthesia.
Antiseptic preparation of the vulva, perineum, and introitus.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Perform bimanual palpation of the vulva and lower vagina to determine the exact margins and depth of the cyst or abscess.
Retract the ipsilateral labium minus laterally to expose the vestibular mucosal surface over the swelling.
Make a vertical incision approximately 2 cm in length over the vestibular mucosa just external to the hymenal ring, avoiding external keratinised labial skin.
Incise through the underlying cyst wall along the same axis to evacuate accumulated mucus or purulent exudate.
Send a microbiological swab of pus for bacterial Gram stain and culture (including testing for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis).
Irrigate the cavity gently with sterile normal saline.
Grasp the edges of the incised cyst wall with fine Allis tissue forceps and evert them outwards.
Suture the cyst wall to the adjacent vestibular mucosa and skin using interrupted absorbable sutures (Vicryl 3-0) to create a permanent open marsupialised pouch.

blocks.title: Complications
bullets: Intraoperative haemorrhage or postoperative vulval haematoma from vascular vestibular tissue.
Secondary wound infection, cellulitis, or premature closure of the marsupialized stoma causing cyst recurrence.
Persistent introital scarring, dyspareunia, or Bartholin fistula.

blocks.title: Post-operative care
bullets: Prescribe oral analgesics and empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics (such as amoxicillin-clavulanate or cephalexin with metronidazole).
Advise warm sitz baths twice daily starting 24 to 48 hours post-procedure to maintain hygiene and promote drainage.
Instruct avoidance of sexual intercourse until the incision is completely epithelialised.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: The incision must always be placed on the inner mucosal aspect of the introitus just outside the hymen, never on the hairy external keratinised labial skin, to prevent visible scarring and painful dyspareunia.
Marsupialisation preserves the secretory lubricating function of the Bartholin gland, which is lost if the gland is completely excised.

viva.q: Why is the incision for Bartholin cyst marsupialisation made on the vestibular mucosal surface rather than the external labium majus?
viva.a: To recreate a physiological opening within the vaginal vestibule at the normal anatomical site of duct opening, promote smooth mucosal drainage, and avoid painful disfiguring scars on the external skin.

viva.q: What is the primary advantage of marsupialisation over complete Bartholin gland excision?
viva.a: Marsupialisation is technically simpler with less bleeding from deep vestibular venous plexuses, carries a low recurrence rate, and preserves the functional secretory lubrication of the Bartholin gland.
